Vulnerable means open to harm in general, while exploitable specifically means open to being used or manipulated for someone else's gain.

examples.everyday: My uncle is too generous, and some of his neighbors see that as an exploitable weakness, so he's learning to say no.
examples.professional: The security team found an exploitable bug in the login page, so we patched it before the release went out.
examples.analytical: A system that rewards short-term gains creates incentives that are exploitable by people willing to cut corners, which is why regulation matters.

nuance.analogy: An exploitable weakness is like an unlocked back door: nothing is broken, but anyone who notices it can walk in.
nuance.etymology: From exploit, from Old French esploit, achievement, from Latin explicitum, unfolded, plus the English suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as EKS-ploit-able, when the stress belongs on ploit.
Using exploitable as a noun in the sense of exploiter, which describes the person doing the taking advantage.

senses.definition: The quality of being expressible.

core.definition: The quality of being able to be put into words or otherwise communicated or represented.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -BIL-, the root of 'possible'. The -ible reduces to 'uh-bul', and the final -ity sounds like 'uh-tee', not 'i-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical or philosophical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy, linguistics, mathematics and AI research, for example when discussing the expressibility of a language or a model. In general speech, people say 'ability to express' or 'capacity to express'. It is a precise word, so use it when you mean whether something can be captured at all, not how vividly.

distinctions.note: Expressibility asks whether something can be put into words or a formal system; expressiveness asks how vividly or powerfully it conveys meaning or feeling.
Expressivity is a technical term in some fields, close to expressiveness; use expressiveness in general English.

examples.everyday: Honestly, a painting like that makes me wonder about the expressibility of grief in paint.
examples.professional: The team questioned the expressibility of our business rules in the current query language, so we switched to a richer one.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein's limits on expressibility, what can be said versus what can only be shown, shape his early philosophy of language.

nuance.analogy: Like asking whether a paper map can show every grain of sand on a beach: some things resist the medium.
nuance.etymology: From express, from Latin exprimere, 'to press out', with the suffixes -ible and -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing expressibility with expressiveness; one asks whether something can be said, the other how well it is said.
Stressing -PRESS- too strongly and making the middle syllables sound like full words.

senses.definition: To edit out (incorrect, offensive, or otherwise undesirable information) from a book or other publication; to cleanse; to purge.
senses.example: The publisher decided to expurgate the love scene from the book, to make it more child-friendly.

senses.definition: To undertake editing out incorrect, offensive, or otherwise undesirable information from (a book or other publication); to cleanse; to purge.
senses.example: The publisher decided to expurgate the book, which meant removing the love scene.

core.definition: To remove objectionable or inappropriate material from a text, book, or film before publication or release.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EKS. The middle syllable is a weak, reduced 'per', and the final 'gate' sounds like 'gayt'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It implies that content was cut, often by censors or editors, which may be seen as a loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expurgate mostly in literary, historical, and academic discussions of censorship, such as an expurgated edition of a classic novel. In everyday speech, people say 'censor,' 'clean up,' or 'edit out.' The word often appears in phrases like 'expurgated edition' or 'expurgated version.'

distinctions.note: Censor is the general term for suppressing material by authority; expurgate specifically means removing parts of a text, often from an edition.
Edit is the neutral, everyday word for changing a text; expurgate means removing content, usually offensive or inappropriate material.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's copy of that old adventure book is expurgated, so some of the rougher scenes are missing.
examples.professional: The publisher wants to expurgate the training manual before sending it to the international team.
examples.analytical: Victorian editors often expurgated the sexual content of classical texts, which distorted the way readers understood those works.

nuance.analogy: To expurgate a book is like trimming a hedge until it looks tidy, but in doing so you cut away branches that were part of the original plant.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expurgare, 'to purify, cleanse', from ex- 'out' plus purgare 'to cleanse'.
common_mistakes: Using expurgate for simply editing or proofreading; it specifically means removing objectionable material.
Stressing the second syllable, as in eks-PUR-gayt.

expurgate.etymology: From Latin *expurgātus*, perfect passive participle of *expurgō* (“purge, cleanse, purify”).

senses.definition: The act of extirpating or uprooting.
senses.example: The city's campaign aimed at the extirpation of invasive kudzu from the riverbanks.

core.definition: The complete removal or destruction of something harmful, such as a disease, a pest, or an entire population, so that none remains.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAY, the third syllable, and the middle syllable 'tir' is a weak r-colored vowel, not 'tear'. The verb extirpate stresses the first syllable (EX-tir-pate), so the stress shifts when the word becomes a noun.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes destruction that is thorough and often deliberate, so it can sound harsh when applied to people or groups.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extirpation mainly in ecology, public health, history and formal writing, for example about a species wiped out in a region or a disease eliminated. In casual talk people say 'wiped out' or 'eradicated' instead. Because it is precise and a little heavy, it works best in reports, articles and academic prose.

distinctions.note: Eradication is broader and more common in everyday and policy talk, often about diseases or problems; extirpation stresses removing every trace, often from a particular area.
Extinction means a species disappears everywhere on Earth; extirpation means it disappears from one region while surviving elsewhere.
Extraction means pulling something out or obtaining it, such as minerals or a tooth; extirpation means destroying or removing something completely.

examples.everyday: My dad is determined to achieve the complete extirpation of dandelions from his lawn.
examples.professional: The extirpation of the duplicate records took three sprints because they were spread across four services.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the extirpation of the bison in the nineteenth century was a deliberate policy or an unintended side effect of settlement.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a weed out by the root, so that nothing grows back from the roots left in the soil.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extirpare, 'to root out', from ex- 'out' and stirps 'stump, root'.
common_mistakes: Using extirpation for simple removal of small things; it implies total destruction, so 'remove the stains' is too strong.
Confusing it with extinction, which refers to a species disappearing everywhere, not to removal from one area.

senses.definition: Something that is extracted or drawn out.
A portion of a book, document, recording etc. incorporated distinctly in another work (for written or spoken words, synonymous to a citation; a quotation).
senses.example: I used an extract of Hemingway's book to demonstrate culture shock.

senses.definition: A decoction, solution, or infusion made by drawing out from any substance that which gives it its essential and characteristic virtue.
senses.example: vanilla extract

senses.definition: Any substance extracted is such a way, and characteristic of that from which it is obtained.
senses.example: quinine is the most important extract of Peruvian bark.

senses.definition: A solid preparation obtained by evaporating a solution of a drug, etc. or the fresh juice of a plant (distinguished from an abstract).
senses.example: The chemist dried the herbal extract into a thick paste that could be measured precisely.

senses.definition: Ancestry; descent.
senses.example: He was of Scottish extract, his grandmother having emigrated from Aberdeen as a young woman.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) A draft or copy of writing; a certified copy of the proceedings in an action and the judgment therein, with an order for execution.
senses.example: The clerk certified an extract of the court's judgment and handed it to the plaintiff's lawyer.

senses.definition: To draw out; to pull out; to remove forcibly from a fixed position, as by traction or suction, etc.
senses.example: to extract a tooth from its socket, a stump from the earth, or a splinter from the finger

senses.definition: To withdraw by squeezing, distillation, or other mechanical or chemical process. Compare abstract (transitive verb).
senses.example: to extract an essential oil from a plant

senses.definition: To pick out; to cite or reproduce a snippet of.
senses.example: extract a passage from a text.

senses.definition: To select parts of a whole.
senses.example: We need to try to extract the positives from the defeat.

senses.definition: To determine (a root of a number).
senses.example: Please extract the cube root of 27.

core.definition: A concentrated substance drawn from a plant, food, or other source, such as vanilla extract, used for flavor or medicine.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, stress the first syllable, EK. As a verb, the stress shifts to the second syllable, ik-STRAKT, so the difference is in stress. The flap t is not used here; the t is a light, clear t at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a product or a passage, not a judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extract most often in cooking and shopping, such as vanilla extract or lemon extract, and in medicine for concentrated plant or herbal products. In academic and professional settings, an extract can be a short passage taken from a book or report. The noun is common, while the verb is more formal.

distinctions.note: Essence is a concentrated liquid used for flavor, often sold in small bottles; extract is more common and can refer to a stronger product or a text passage.
Excerpt is a passage taken from a longer text, while extract can also mean a product or a removed substance.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the vanilla extract from the cabinet? The recipe calls for a teaspoon.
examples.professional: Please include the short extract from the vendor's report in the appendix of our presentation.
examples.analytical: The essay uses a brief extract from Augustine to illustrate the argument about divine grace.

nuance.analogy: Like brewing a strong tea from loose leaves: the essential flavor is drawn out and concentrated.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extrahere, to draw out, from ex- (out) and trahere (to draw).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable in the noun, which makes it sound like the verb.
Using extract when you mean excerpt; extract often suggests a selected passage, but both can be used for written text.

extract.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *extractum*, neuter perfect passive participle of *extrahō*, from *ex-* + *trahō*.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or accompanied by exudation.
senses.example: The doctor noted exudative patches on the inflamed tissue, a sign of infection.

core.definition: Characterized by or producing exudate, especially fluid that seeps out of inflamed or damaged tissue. Used in medicine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZOO. The -ative ending is short and unstressed, sounding like 'tiv', not 'tayv'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exudative mostly in medical settings, such as describing pleural effusions or types of macular degeneration. A physician might say 'exudative macular degeneration' to mean the wet form of the disease. Patients rarely use the word; they would say 'the wet kind' or 'leaking fluid'.

distinctions.note: Transudative fluid leaks out because of pressure or fluid imbalance without inflammation, while exudative fluid leaks because of inflamed or damaged tissue.

examples.everyday: My uncle has the wet kind of macular degeneration, which doctors call exudative.
examples.professional: The pathology report flagged the lesion as exudative, so we'll need a follow-up biopsy.
examples.analytical: Distinguishing transudative from exudative effusions depends on protein content and cell count in the fluid.

nuance.analogy: Like a pipe that leaks because its wall is cracked, an exudative process leaks because the tissue itself is damaged or inflamed.
nuance.etymology: From exudate, from Latin exsudare 'to sweat out', plus the suffix -ative.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adjective exudative with the noun exudate.
Using exudative to describe ordinary leaking objects instead of inflamed or damaged tissue.

senses.definition: Vision or the faculty of sight.
senses.example: good eyesight

senses.definition: View or the range of vision.
senses.example: The eye doctor said my eyesight had worsened, so I needed stronger glasses.

core.definition: The ability of your eyes to see; how clearly you can see with them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on EYE, and the final syllable has a long i, like the word site. Do not reduce the second part to a weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; losing eyesight sounds serious, so the word can carry concern when used about illness or aging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eyesight in everyday talk about vision, especially for older people or for sports and driving. Phrases like her eyesight is getting worse or I have terrible eyesight sound natural. Vision is the more clinical word, and eyesight feels more personal.

distinctions.note: Vision is more formal and can also mean a future plan; eyesight is everyday and refers to physical seeing.
Sight is the general word and can also mean a view or a famous place; eyesight specifically means the ability to see.

examples.everyday: My grandpa still has pretty good eyesight, so he reads the paper without his glasses.
examples.professional: The safety training requires that all forklift drivers pass an eyesight check before they start.
examples.analytical: Scripture links physical eyesight with spiritual perception, so Isaac's failing eyesight in Genesis becomes a figure for limited understanding.

nuance.analogy: Eyesight is like the lens of a camera: when it is clean and sharp, the picture is clear.
nuance.etymology: Eye (Old English eage) plus sight (Old English gesiht), from the sense of seeing.
common_mistakes: Spelling it eyesite; the correct spelling is eyesight.
Using eyesight for a single view; for a view or a famous place, the word is sight.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word for eye is 'ayin, which often stands for sight and perception. Deuteronomy 34:7 says Moses's eye was not dim when he died, a sign of lasting strength. Genesis 27:1 says Isaac's eyes were dim with age, so he could not reliably see who stood before him. 1 Samuel 3:2 notes that Eli's eyes had begun to grow dim, so he could not see.

senses.definition: Identifying or verifying a person from their face.

core.definition: Technology that identifies or verifies a person by analyzing the features of their face in an image or video.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on NISH in 'recognition,' and 'facial' has a secondary stress on FAY. Americans say 'FAY-shul,' with the vowel reduced, not 'fa-see-al.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical settings, but often debated because of privacy and fairness concerns.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use facial recognition for software that matches faces, for example to unlock a phone or to identify people in images. In news and policy debates it often carries concerns about surveillance and bias. For a phone unlock feature, Americans may say Face ID, which is Apple's brand name.

distinctions.note: Face detection only finds that a face is present, while facial recognition identifies or verifies who the person is.
Biometrics is the broader category of identifying people by physical traits, and facial recognition is one kind of biometric method.

examples.everyday: My phone uses facial recognition to unlock, so I don't have to type a passcode.
examples.professional: Our model's facial recognition accuracy dropped for older users, so we're retraining it with more data.
examples.analytical: Facial recognition raises questions about consent, surveillance, and whether error rates fall unevenly across groups.

nuance.analogy: Facial recognition works like a doorman who matches each face against a guest list, but it does so with numbers instead of memory.
nuance.etymology: Facial comes from Latin facies 'face'; recognition comes from Latin recognoscere 'to know again.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'recognition of facial' instead of 'facial recognition.'
Confusing it with face detection, which finds faces but does not identify them.

conversation.text: Facial recognition matches a face in an image against a database of known faces.
Some facial recognition systems have shown higher error rates for certain demographic groups.
Several cities have debated limits on police use of facial recognition.

senses.definition: In existentialism, the state of being in the world without any knowable reason for such existence, or of being in a particular state of affairs which one has no control over.
senses.example: In her philosophy seminar, she argued that our facticity limits what we can choose to become.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being a fact.
senses.example: The judge questioned the facticity of the witness's claim before admitting the document.

senses.definition: A fact that is not changeable or that is assumed to be true without further evaluation.
senses.example: Our team stopped treating last year's churn rates as a settled facticity and reran the numbers.

core.definition: In existentialist philosophy, the given facts of one's situation, such as birth, body, and circumstances, that one did not choose but must live within.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TIS, and the final syllable is a reduced 'tee'. Americans say the middle syllable with a quick, weak vowel, not a full 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term that describes conditions without judging them.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized philosophical term, most used in existentialist and phenomenological writing by Sartre, Heidegger, and their interpreters. Outside philosophy, Americans would say 'the facts' or 'the way things are'. In a seminar or academic paper, it is precise and natural; in ordinary talk it would sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: 'Factuality' is the general quality of being factual; 'facticity' in existentialism refers to the unchosen conditions that limit a person's freedom.
Contingency means that something could have been otherwise; facticity means the fixed conditions one actually faces and must take up.

examples.everyday: I know I can't change where I was born, so I just accept that part of my life as a given.
examples.professional: In our ethics seminar, we discussed how a team's facticity, its budget and history, shapes what decisions are actually possible.
examples.analytical: Sartre argues that human freedom operates within facticity, so that our choices are made from a situation we did not select.

nuance.analogy: Facticity is like the table of cards you are dealt in a game: you cannot choose the hand, but you still decide how to play it.
nuance.etymology: Coined in English from 'fact', from Latin factum, 'thing done', with the suffix '-ity'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'factuality' in everyday contexts, where it sounds too technical.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly, as 'fak-TIH-sih-tee'.

facticity.etymology: From *fact* + *icity*, possibly modelled on German *Faktizität* which first appeared in the writings of the German philosopher Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814).

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or caused by factions.
senses.example: The factious rivalry between the two departments delayed the software release for months.

senses.definition: Given to or characterized by discordance or insubordination.
senses.example: The factious board members refused every compromise and kept interrupting the chairman.

core.definition: Causing or characterized by division, conflict, or rebellion within a group, especially by stirring up disagreement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, FAK, and the ending is a quick 'shus'. Keep the 'ch' sound out of it, since it is 'sh' as in 'ocean'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes people who deliberately create division or resist authority.
nuance.usage_note: This word appears mainly in formal writing, political commentary, and history. Americans would more often say 'divisive' or 'disruptive' in everyday speech. Calling a colleague 'factious' in a meeting would sound harsh and old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Divisive' is common and describes something that splits people apart; 'factious' implies deliberate stirring up of rival groups.
'Disruptive' is general and everyday; 'factious' is more specific to political or group conflict.

examples.everyday: Stop being so factious at dinner; we are all on the same side.
examples.professional: The manager asked the team to stop the factious arguments and focus on the shared launch goal.
examples.analytical: Hobbes saw the factious spirit of groups within the commonwealth as a threat to peace and sovereignty.

nuance.analogy: A factious group is like a family that keeps picking fights to split the household into camps.
nuance.etymology: From Latin factiosus, 'of a faction', from factio, 'party or group'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'fictitious', which means made up or false.
Using it for simple disagreement; it implies deliberate division.

factious.etymology: From Latin *factiosus* (“divisive; inclined to separate”); derivative of *factio*.

senses.definition: A perjurer; a deceptive or misleading witness.
senses.example: The judge warned that a false witness could face prison for perjury under federal law.

senses.definition: Deceptive public statements.
senses.example: to bear false witness

core.definition: A person who gives false or misleading testimony, especially under oath or in court, in order to deceive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WIT in witness, and the final -ness is reduced to nus. The tn in witness is usually a syllabic n, so do not insert an extra uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It implies deliberate deception that harms someone, especially in court or in a moral context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use false witness mostly in legal, religious and moral discussions, and in the Ten Commandments phrase bear false witness. In everyday talk people say liar, he was lying, or he lied under oath. Calling a friend a false witness in casual conversation would sound dramatic or formal.

distinctions.note: A perjurer is someone who lies under oath, which is a specific legal offense; a false witness can be anyone who deceives in testimony, even outside a formal oath.
An eyewitness saw an event directly and may be honest but wrong; a false witness deliberately gives a misleading account.

examples.everyday: My cousin swore he saw me at the game, but he's a terrible false witness; I was home all afternoon.
examples.professional: The deposition revealed that the plaintiff's assistant had been a false witness, so the attorneys asked the court to strike her testimony.
examples.analytical: The commandment against bearing false witness condemns not only perjury in court but any deception that damages a neighbor's reputation.

nuance.analogy: Like a scale tipped by a hidden weight: the verdict looks balanced, but the evidence was rigged from the start.
nuance.etymology: Witness comes from Old English witnes, knowledge or testimony, from witan to know; false comes from Latin falsus, deceived or untrue.
common_mistakes: Using false witness for an honest mistake; the term implies deliberate deception.
Using a false witness with the wrong preposition: say a false witness against someone, not a false witness to someone, when the testimony harms them.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew phrase behind this idea is ʿēd shāqer (ʿēd, witness; shāqer, falsehood or lying), used of someone who testifies untruthfully. The commandment in Exodus 20:16 forbids giving false testimony against a neighbor, and Deuteronomy 5:20 repeats it when Moses recalls the law. Proverbs 19:5 warns that a false witness will not go unpunished, showing that God takes deceit in legal testimony seriously.

senses.definition: Known to one, or generally known; commonplace.
senses.example: There’s a familiar face; that tune sounds familiar.

senses.definition: Acquainted.
senses.example: I'm quite familiar with this system; she's not familiar with manual gears.

senses.definition: Intimate or friendly.
senses.example: We are on familiar terms now; our neighbor is not familiar

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a family; familial.
An attendant spirit, often in animal or demon form.
senses.example: The witch’s familiar was a black cat.

senses.definition: A member of a pope's or bishop's household.
(historical) The officer of the Inquisition who arrested suspected people.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Known to you or easy to recognize because you have seen, heard or experienced it before.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MIL. The final '-iar' is pronounced as a single reduced syllable 'yer', not 'ee-ar' or 'fa-mil-ee-ar'. The 'r' is pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or neutral, meaning comfortable and recognizable. It turns negative when used for behavior that is too forward, as in 'too familiar'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use familiar constantly for things that feel recognizable ('That song sounds familiar') and for people they know ('I'm familiar with her work'). Saying 'You look familiar' is a common, friendly opener. 'Too familiar' signals inappropriate closeness, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Intimate suggests deep personal closeness; familiar is broader and can describe knowledge of a thing as well as a person.
Common means something happens or exists often; familiar means it is known to you, which may not be common for others.

examples.everyday: Your face looks familiar, have we met at the gym?
examples.professional: This deployment process is familiar to most of the team, so we can skip the onboarding slides.
examples.analytical: The author draws on a familiar distinction between appearance and reality, but reworks it in an unexpected way.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-worn trail through the woods: you can walk it in the dark because you already know every turn.
nuance.etymology: From Latin familiaris, of the household, from familia, household.
common_mistakes: Using 'familiar of' or 'familiar at'; the usual prepositions are 'familiar with' and, less often, 'familiar to'.
Adding a syllable, pronouncing it 'fa-MIL-ee-ar' with three full vowels; the ending is a single reduced syllable.

familiar.etymology: From Middle English *familiar,familier*, from Latin *familiāris* (“pertaining to servants; pertaining to the household”).

senses.definition: (dated) A mobile phone that has some advanced capabilities but is not as powerful as a smartphone.
senses.example: My dad still uses a feature phone with a tiny screen, mostly just for calls and texting.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A basic mobile phone with limited features, a small screen, and few or no apps, unlike a smartphone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, FEE-cher, and keep the second word lighter. The final syllable of 'feature' is a rhotic 'cher,' not 'choor.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly dated. It can sound slightly condescending if used to describe someone's old phone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'flip phone,' 'basic phone,' or 'dumb phone' for these devices. 'Feature phone' is more common in the phone industry and in reports about developing markets. Calling someone's phone a feature phone could sound like a mild dig, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: A flip phone is a folding phone, which may or may not be a feature phone; the term describes shape, while feature phone describes capability.
A smartphone runs apps and connects to the internet, while a feature phone has only basic functions.

examples.everyday: My dad still uses a feature phone that only does calls and texts, and he likes it that way.
examples.professional: Our emerging-markets team sells mostly to feature phone users, so the app must work offline.
examples.analytical: The feature phone shows how mobile communication existed before app ecosystems redefined the device.

nuance.analogy: Like a pocketknife with only a few blades compared with a full multi-tool.
nuance.etymology: 'Feature' is from Old French 'faiture'; 'phone' is from Greek 'phōnē,' meaning sound or voice.
common_mistakes: Calling a smartphone a feature phone, which sounds inaccurate to people in tech.
Pronouncing 'feature' with an extra syllable, as in 'FEE-tchur.'

feature-phone.etymology: From being a feature-rich cellphone, more capable than prior iterations of mobile phones.

senses.definition: Someone or something that feels.
senses.example: Are you more of a feeler or more of a thinker?

senses.definition: Something ventured to test another's feelings, opinion, or position.
senses.example: I sent out some feelers but they didn't seem interested.

senses.definition: An antenna or appendage used for feeling, especially on an insect.
senses.example: The moth brushed the lamp with its feeler, testing the warm air before landing on the sill.

core.definition: Something you say or do to test someone's opinion, interest or reaction before committing to a decision or plan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the 'ee' long. The second syllable is unstressed and the 'r' is clear, so say it 'FEE-lur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a cautious test and carries no negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say put out a feeler or put out feelers to describe testing the waters, such as asking a boss about a raise or a company about a job. It is informal but common in both business and everyday talk. For the physical sense of an insect antenna, the word is used mainly in biology or nature writing.

distinctions.note: A probe is a more thorough, sometimes investigative inquiry, while a feeler is a light, tentative test of opinion.
Test the waters is an idiom with a similar meaning; put out feelers is slightly more formal and emphasizes the indirect approach.

examples.everyday: I put out a feeler to my brother about moving to Denver, and he said he'd be happy to have us nearby.
examples.professional: Before we commit to the contract, I'd like to send a feeler to the vendor about their pricing for a larger volume.
examples.analytical: The early papers were feelers, tentative proposals that tested whether the field would accept the claim before the authors committed to it.

nuance.analogy: A feeler is like a fishing line with a small bait: you cast it lightly to see whether anything bites before you commit your whole net.
nuance.etymology: From feel (Old English fēlan) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'put out feelers' with 'to make feelers', which is not idiomatic.
Using feeler for a serious, formal proposal; it implies a tentative test, not a firm offer.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to feudalism.

core.definition: Relating to feudalism, the medieval system in which land was granted to lords in exchange for loyalty and military service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second syllable as a weak 'dul,' not 'dahl.' The first vowel sounds like the word 'few.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical discussion. In modern commentary, it is often negative, as in 'feudal management' meaning rigid, inherited power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'feudal' in history classes, political analysis, and writing about medieval society. Outside those settings, it is often used metaphorically for an unfair, rigid system, and this can sound pointed or critical. Say 'a feudal system' or 'feudal lords' when describing history.

distinctions.note: 'Medieval' names a whole historical era, while 'feudal' names one specific social and legal system within it.
'Manorial' refers to the manor, the local estate; 'feudal' covers the wider system of land and obligations among lords and vassals.
'Autocratic' describes absolute personal rule, whereas 'feudal' describes a decentralized hierarchy of obligations.

examples.everyday: My history teacher said the feudal system ended slowly, not all at once.
examples.professional: Our internal approval process is so feudal that every team lead controls their own budget with no oversight.
examples.analytical: Marc Bloch argued that feudal society was defined less by a single institution than by a web of personal dependence and mutual obligation.

nuance.analogy: A feudal system is like a pyramid of favors: each person owes service upward and receives protection downward.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin feudalis, from feudum, meaning fief or land held in exchange for service.
common_mistakes: Using 'feudal' as a noun; the noun is 'feudalism.'
Saying 'FOO-dal' with the vowel of 'food' in the first syllable; it sounds like 'few.'

feudal.etymology: From Old French *feodal*, from Medieval Latin *feodalis*, from *feodum*, *feudum*, *fevum* (“fief, fee”), from **fehu* (“cattle, owndom, property, fee”), from Proto-Germanic **fehu* (“cattle”).

senses.definition: A form of hockey played on a grassed pitch with a hard rubber ball instead of a puck.

core.definition: A team sport played on a grass pitch with curved sticks and a small hard ball, not on ice.

pronunciation.tip: Compound nouns usually put the main stress on the first word, so say FIELD clearly and keep the second word lighter. The vowel in HOCK is the 'o' of 'hot', not 'hope', and the final -ey is a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain sports term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly associate field hockey with a women's sport taught in high schools and colleges, though men's programs exist. In the US, 'hockey' alone usually means ice hockey, so add 'field' when the context could be unclear. Americans rarely abbreviate it in speech.

distinctions.note: Played on ice with skates and a puck; in the US, 'hockey' alone normally means this.
Also a stick-and-ball sport, but lacrosse sticks have a net pocket for catching and throwing, while field hockey players hit the ball.

examples.everyday: My daughter plays field hockey, so our Saturdays are basically spent at the school field.
examples.professional: Our company sponsors the local high school field hockey league, so we're hosting the spring tournament.
examples.analytical: Field hockey's rules on stick height reflect an ongoing tension between skill, speed and player safety.

nuance.analogy: Like ice hockey moved onto grass, with a ball in place of the puck.
nuance.etymology: Hockey from Anglo-French hoquet, a shepherd's crook; 'field' names the outdoor pitch.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I play hockey' without context, which Americans hear as ice hockey.
Pronouncing hockey with the vowel of 'hope' (HOH-kee) instead of the vowel of 'hot' (HAH-kee).

senses.definition: Of or relating to fire.
Burning or glowing.
Inflammable or easily ignited.
senses.example: Solvents with fiery vapors should never be stored near the water heater.

senses.definition: Having the color of fire.
senses.example: The sunset painted the sky in fiery shades of orange and red.

senses.definition: Hot or inflamed.
senses.example: The fiery rash on his wrist made the nurse call the doctor right away.

senses.definition: Tempestuous or emotionally volatile; sulfurous.
senses.example: a fiery temper

senses.definition: Spirited or filled with emotion.
senses.example: She gave a fiery speech that had the whole union cheering.

senses.definition: Having the capillaries contracted due to stress at time of slaughter, causing blood to not drain properly.
senses.example: The meat inspector rejected the carcasses because they looked fiery and poorly bled.

core.definition: Literally burning or glowing like fire; figuratively, passionate, angry or full of energy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is quick, and the final -y is a light 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive when praising passion, energy or spirit; negative when describing anger or a hot temper.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fiery for a spicy food, a red sunset, a passionate speech or a temper. It is common in everyday talk: 'That chili is fiery' is natural. Describing a person as fiery usually suggests strong emotion and is generally polite.

distinctions.note: Passionate describes deep feeling in general, while fiery adds a sense of visible heat, energy or temper.
Spicy describes food flavor; fiery can describe food, but also emotion, color or speech.

examples.everyday: That salsa is so fiery that I needed a glass of milk right away.
examples.professional: She gave a fiery presentation that convinced the leadership team to fund the project.
examples.analytical: The prophet's fiery language draws on imagery of burning altars and purifying flame.

nuance.analogy: A fiery speech is like a campfire that spreads its heat across the whole room.
nuance.etymology: From fire, from Old English fyr, meaning fire.
common_mistakes: Saying 'FY-ree' with the wrong vowel; the middle syllable is 'ur' as in 'fire'.
Using fiery for a cold or calm person, which sounds contradictory.
nuance.biblical_note: Fiery in Scripture often describes God's presence, judgment or the spiritual battle, using the Hebrew word saraph, meaning to burn. Numbers 21:6 describes fiery serpents sent among the Israelites in the wilderness. Deuteronomy 8:15 recalls the same wilderness and its fiery serpents, while Ephesians 6:16 speaks of the flaming darts of the evil one that faith can quench.

fiery.etymology: From Middle English *fyry*, from *fyr* (“fire”), equivalent to *fire* + *-y*.

senses.definition: A tactic (such as giving long, often irrelevant speeches) employed to delay the proceedings of, or the making of a decision by, a legislative body, particularly the United States Senate.
senses.example: The senator's twelve-hour filibuster delayed the vote until nearly midnight.

senses.definition: A member of a legislative body causing such an obstruction.

(historical) A mercenary soldier; a freebooter; specifically, a mercenary who traveled illegally in an organized group from the United States to a country in Central America or the Spanish West Indies in the mid-19th century seeking economic and political benefits through armed force.
senses.example: Nineteenth-century filibuster bands sailed from New Orleans hoping to seize land in Central America.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To take part in a private military action in a foreign country.
senses.example: Several American adventurers planned to filibuster in Nicaragua before the government stopped them.

senses.definition: To use obstructionist tactics in a legislative body.
senses.example: Republicans threatened to filibuster the nominee unless leaders agreed to hold a hearing.

core.definition: A tactic in a legislative body, especially the U.S. Senate, in which a member prolongs debate to block a vote.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is 'ster', with the r pronounced and the vowel reduced, not 'boo-ster'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, depending on the speaker's politics; supporters call it a defense of minority rights and critics call it obstruction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use filibuster mainly in news and political talk about the Senate, where the 60-vote threshold for cloture ends most filibusters. Saying 'they are filibustering' is common during heated debates. The word is not used for ordinary meetings, though people may jokingly say someone is filibustering a conversation.

distinctions.note: Debate is a normal exchange of arguments; a filibuster is a deliberate strategy to delay a decision.
Obstruction is a broader term for blocking progress; a filibuster is a specific parliamentary tactic.

examples.everyday: The Senate has been stuck on that bill because of a filibuster.
examples.professional: Our project review got bogged down by a filibuster of comments that kept repeating the same objection.
examples.analytical: The filibuster illustrates how procedural rules can shape substantive policy outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Like someone holding the microphone for hours so the meeting cannot end.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch vrijbuiter (freebooter), via Spanish and French, originally meaning a pirate or mercenary.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'boo-ster'.
Using it as a verb about any long meeting without the legislative sense.

filibuster.etymology: Spanish *filibustero* (“pirate”), from French *flibustier*, ultimately from Dutch *vrijbuiter* (“freebooter”), from *vrij* (“free”) + *buit* (“booty”) + *-er* (“agent”).

senses.definition: Any particle that has been removed by a file or similar implement; a shaving.
senses.example: The process left metal filings all over the bench and the part.

senses.definition: The act of storing documents in an archive; archiving.
Something that has been officially filed; a document on file.
senses.example: The clerk pulled the old filing from the cabinet and handed me a copy.

core.definition: The work of putting documents in order and storing them in folders, cabinets, or electronic systems so they can be found later.

pronunciation.tip: The stress and vowel are on FY, a diphthong like the word my. Do not say FILL-ing, which is a different word meaning something that fills.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes routine administrative work and can sound tedious in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use filing for organizing paper or digital records, and also for submitting official forms, as in tax filing. In offices people often say 'I need to do some filing' or 'the filing is due Friday.' The word is common in both everyday and professional talk.

distinctions.note: A file is the folder, document, or digital record itself, while filing is the act or system of organizing and storing it.
Filings in the plural means tiny metal particles from a file tool, a different sense from the office meaning.

examples.everyday: I have to finish my tax filing this weekend, or I'll be stuck with a penalty.
examples.professional: Our team cut the filing backlog by moving everything to the shared drive.
examples.analytical: The historian studied how medieval clerks' filing systems shaped the way records were preserved.

nuance.analogy: Filing is like keeping a well-organized kitchen pantry: everything has a place, so you can find it quickly when you need it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb file, originally 'to string papers on a thread,' from Old French fil, 'thread.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the pronunciation with filling, which has a short i sound.
Using filing to mean a single document; a file is the correct word for one record.
Writing 'I did the filings' when you mean the office task; the usual phrase is 'I did the filing.'

senses.definition: The quality of being finicky.

core.definition: The quality of being finicky, or overly fussy and hard to please about small details.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The -y of finicky changes to -iness, which is pronounced ee-nus, and the middle syllable is short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone is hard to please and may be exhausting to deal with.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use finicky about eaters, cats, or people who are particular about routines. Finickiness is the noun form and is common in conversation about food, habits, or work standards. It can be used lightly, but it may annoy the person described if said directly to them.

distinctions.note: Pickiness is a very everyday word and is common with food. Finickiness suggests extreme attention and is slightly stronger.
Finicky is the adjective used in most conversation. Finickiness is the abstract noun for the quality.

examples.everyday: Her finickiness about her coffee order drives the barista crazy.
examples.professional: The client's finickiness over fonts pushed our timeline back by a week.
examples.analytical: The finickiness of his editorial standards made him a superb proofreader and an exhausting colleague.

nuance.analogy: Finickiness is like a thermostat set to exactly one degree that keeps being adjusted, never quite satisfied.
nuance.etymology: From finicky, from finick.
common_mistakes: Spelling it finickyness; the y changes to i before -ness.
Using it for a positive attention to detail without a negative tone.

core.definition: Describing the earliest ripened fruit of a season, such as figs or grapes, which the Bible treats as especially prized and dedicated to God.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FIRST in this hyphenated compound, with ripe lighter. Pronounce the vowel in ripe as a long i diphthong, like 'ryp', not 'reep'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests early blessing and promise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word outside Bible study, sermons and religious writing. In ordinary talk people say 'the first ripe figs' or 'early figs.' Use it when you are discussing the Bible or the agriculture of ancient Israel.

distinctions.note: Firstfruits is the offering or the harvest itself; first-ripe describes a fruit or crop as the earliest to ripen.
Early is a general word for before the usual time; first-ripe is specific to the first fruit of a season in biblical language.

examples.everyday: Grandma's fig tree gave us the first-ripe figs of the summer, and she made us save a few for the church picnic.
examples.professional: The preacher explained the first-ripe offering in Numbers, and some of the youth group had never heard the term before.
examples.analytical: The prophet's image of first-ripe figs presents Israel as a rare and desired fruit that the Lord notices early, before the rest of the harvest.

nuance.analogy: Like the first peach from a backyard tree in June, which tastes better than the ones that follow.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fyrst, 'first', and ripe, from Old English ripe, 'ready to be harvested'.
common_mistakes: Using first-ripe as a noun, when it is normally an adjective before a noun
Stressing ripe instead of first in the compound
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word bikkurah (bikkurah), meaning first-ripe fruit, appears in the Old Testament for the first produce of a harvest that belonged to the Lord. Numbers 13:20 describes the season of the first-ripe grapes when the spies entered the land. Isaiah 28:4 compares a people's early fate to a first-ripe fig that is eaten as soon as it is seen. Hosea 9:10 recalls God's delight in Israel as the first-ripe fruit on the fig tree, and then describes how Israel turned away to shameful idols.

senses.definition: The most important one out of a related group.
senses.example: The retail company's store in London is their flagship.

senses.definition: The ship occupied by the fleet's commander (usually an admiral); it denotes this by flying his flag.
senses.example: The admiral raised his flag aboard the flagship, leading the fleet into harbor.

senses.definition: The ship regarded as most important out of a group, e.g. a nation's navy or company's fleet.
To act as a flagship for.
senses.example: The new hospital will flagship the regional network of clinics for the state.

core.definition: The most important, best-known or leading product, store or ship in a company's or organization's group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FLAG. The g is hard, the sh sound begins the second syllable, and you should not insert a vowel between g and sh.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals prestige, importance and brand pride, and it can sound corporate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flagship constantly in business news, marketing and retail, for a company's main store, a brand's top product or a university's main campus. It also refers to a navy's lead ship. In casual conversation people may say main or best one, but in business talk flagship is natural.

distinctions.note: Headquarters is the central office where a company is managed, while a flagship is an important store, product or branch that represents the brand.
Signature describes a feature typical of a brand, while flagship describes the top product or outlet in its lineup.

examples.everyday: We went to the flagship Target downtown because it's bigger than the one near our house.
examples.professional: The flagship app drives most of our revenue, so the team is prioritizing its performance this quarter.
examples.analytical: The state university's flagship campus shapes public identity, so its policies carry symbolic weight beyond the classroom.

nuance.analogy: A flagship is like the lead boat in a fleet: the others follow its course and show its colors.
nuance.etymology: From flag, a naval banner, and ship; the ship that carries the admiral's flag.
common_mistakes: Using flagship only for ships; in American business it is common for stores, products and campuses.
Writing flag ship as two words; the standard form is one word.

senses.definition: Showing disrespect through a casual attitude, levity, and a lack of due seriousness; pert.
senses.example: Her flippant reply to the grieving widow shocked everyone at the funeral.

senses.definition: Loquacious; speaking with ease and rapidity.
senses.example: The flippant talker at the party kept the whole table laughing with stories.

senses.definition: Nimble; limber.
senses.example: The flippant dancer slipped between the chairs with quick, light footwork.

core.definition: Showing a careless, disrespectful attitude, especially when a serious matter deserves respect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLIP. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so say it as a quick un, and do not add an extra vowel before the final t.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a tone or remark that seems careless or rude about something important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flippant to criticize casual remarks made at the wrong time, such as a joke at a funeral or a dismissive answer to a serious question. It is stronger than casual and suggests disrespect. People often say that is flippant or don't be flippant when they want someone to be serious.

distinctions.note: Playful is friendly and light, while flippant suggests a careless or disrespectful dismissal of something that matters.
Casual describes an relaxed manner, while flippant adds the sense of disrespect toward serious matters.

examples.everyday: Don't be flippant when I tell you the doctor called, because it's serious.
examples.professional: His flippant reply to the security concern made the review meeting tense.
examples.analytical: The philosopher calls such flippant dismissals of conscience a failure of moral seriousness.

nuance.analogy: A flippant remark is like skipping a step on a staircase: it looks quick, but it misses what matters.
nuance.etymology: From an earlier sense meaning nimble or talkative, from Latin roots for light or quick.
common_mistakes: Using flippant to mean fun or cheerful without any disrespect.
Confusing flippant with frivolous, which means silly or unimportant rather than disrespectful.

flippant.etymology: 1595, from Northern English dialectal *flippand* (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of *flip* (“to babble”), of origin.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A flip-flop.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: (uncommon) A rapid or unpredictable shift in behavior.
senses.example: His constant flippy-flop on the budget left his team unsure which plan was real.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: An informal, childish name for a flip-flop sandal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FLIP, and make the middle syllable a short 'ee' sound. The final syllable uses the short, open vowel of 'lot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It sounds childlike or cute, so it fits family talk better than professional writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans, especially parents and kids, use this playful variant of flip-flop. Adults usually say flip-flops in ordinary speech. Using it in a meeting or formal email would sound unusual, though a friendly joke can make it work.

distinctions.note: Flip-flop is the standard word used by almost all adults; flippy-flop is a playful, childish variant.
Sandal is the broad category; flippy-flop is a specific, informal name for one kind.

examples.everyday: My grandson insists on calling his flip-flops flippy-flops.
examples.professional: In the dress-code email, I wrote 'no flippy-flops' as a joke, and the team laughed.
examples.analytical: The playful name flippy-flop shows how casual speech reshapes familiar words.

nuance.analogy: Like a nickname for a pet: the same animal, but with a name that shows affection and a bit of silliness.
common_mistakes: Using it in a formal setting where flip-flop is expected.
Confusing it with the verb flip-flop, which means to change one's position repeatedly.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or characteristic of flowers.
senses.example: The flowery meadow behind the farmhouse was buzzing with bees in late May.

senses.definition: Decorated with or abundant in flowers.
Of a speech or piece of writing: overly complicated or elaborate; with grandiloquent expressions; marked by rhetorical elegance.
senses.example: The senator's speech was so flowery that half the audience lost track of his point.

senses.definition: Melodramatic, overexaggerated.
senses.example: She gave a flowery account of the accident that made it sound like a movie.

senses.definition: A flowery person.
senses.example: Our new manager is a flowery who never says anything plainly.

senses.definition: A flowery phrase or statement.
senses.example: His wedding toast was full of flowery phrases about love and destiny.

senses.definition: A flowery decoration.
senses.example: The cake had a few flowery decorations piped around the edges.

senses.definition: Diminutive of flower.
senses.example: The toddler proudly showed me the tiny flowery she had picked from the lawn.

senses.definition: (rare) Someone or something considered flowery.
senses.example: Nobody expected the blunt engineer to be such a flowery.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) A place where flowers grow.
senses.example: The old abbey grounds became a flowery where bees gathered each summer.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Using too many fancy, showy or elaborate words and images, especially in speech or writing; also decorated with flowers or flower patterns.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The first vowel sounds like the ow in how, not the o in go, so it sounds like flower. The final -y is a short ee sound, and the r is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Mostly mildly negative when describing language, suggesting excess or insincerity; neutral or positive when describing physical decoration such as flowery fabric or wallpaper.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use flowery to criticize speech or writing that is overwrought, as in flowery language or a flowery toast that goes on too long. For physical flower patterns, Americans more often say floral, as in a floral dress. In professional writing, plain language or purple prose (for especially ornate writing) are common alternatives.

distinctions.note: Ornate describes elaborate decoration in objects, buildings or style; flowery describes language or writing with showy, florid phrasing.
Florid is stronger and suggests excessive, ostentatious ornament or a reddish complexion; flowery is milder and more common for everyday speech criticism.
Floral describes a flower pattern or flower-related thing neutrally, while flowery is used for showy language or heavily decorated surfaces.

examples.everyday: Don't give me all the flowery language; just tell me if the car is fixed.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal was full of flowery claims, so I asked for specific metrics in plain terms.
examples.analytical: The sermon's flowery style concealed a thin argument, making the rhetoric seem more substantial than the reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Flowery speech is like a garden path lined with so many blossoms that you forget where it leads.
nuance.etymology: From flower plus the suffix -y, meaning full of or resembling; flower comes from Old French flor, from Latin flos.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel like the o in flow (/floʊ/) instead of the ow in how (/aʊ/).
Using flowery for simple flower patterns, where Americans usually say floral.

senses.definition: A sport played on foot in which teams attempt to get a ball into a goal or zone defended by the other team.
senses.example: Roman and medieval football matches were more violent than any modern type of football.

senses.definition: The ball used in any game called "football".
senses.example: The player kicked the football.

senses.definition: American football: a game played on a field 100 yards long and 53 1/3 yards wide in which two teams of 11 players attempt to get an ovoid ball to the end of each other's territory.
senses.example: Each team scored two touchdowns when they played football.

senses.definition: Canadian football: a game played on a field 110 yards long and 65 yards wide in which two teams of 12 players attempt to get an ovoid ball to the end of each other's territory.
senses.example: They played football in the snow.

senses.definition: Any form of rugby. rugby league.
senses.example: In Sydney, football usually means rugby league rather than soccer, which confused me at first.

senses.definition: Practice of these particular games, or techniques used in them.
senses.example: Her coaching focuses on football fundamentals like footwork, tackling technique, and field position.

senses.definition: An item of discussion, particularly in a back-and-forth manner.
senses.example: That budget item became a political football.

senses.definition: The leather briefcase containing classified nuclear war plans which is always near the US President.
senses.example: The military aide carried the football everywhere the president traveled, never more than steps away.

senses.definition: (rare) To play football.
senses.example: They spent the afternoon footballing on the muddy field until it got too dark to see.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: In the United States, a sport played by two teams of eleven players on a field, using an oval ball and a goal line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FUT. The second syllable is a light 'ball' with a vowel close to 'aw', so say 'FUT-bawl'. Do not stress both syllables equally.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common sport name that is often associated with American culture, especially on weekends and holidays.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'football' means American football unless the context says otherwise. For the sport most of the world calls football, Americans say 'soccer'. If you say 'football' to mean soccer, people will think you mean the NFL. You can say 'Are you watching football this weekend?' in casual talk, and 'the big football game' often refers to a college or NFL contest.

distinctions.note: 'Soccer' is the American word for the sport played with feet and no hand contact; 'football' in the US means American football.
'Rugby' is a different sport with an oval ball and no forward passing; Americans sometimes mistake it for football.

examples.everyday: Do you want to come over and watch football on Sunday?
examples.professional: Our marketing team is sponsoring the college football bowl game this December.
examples.analytical: Sociologists have argued that American football functions as a civic ritual that brings together regional and class identities.

nuance.analogy: Football is like a chess match on a field: every play is a planned move, and the teams are constantly testing each other's strategy.
nuance.etymology: From 'foot' and 'ball', originally referring to games played on foot rather than on horseback.
common_mistakes: Using 'football' to mean soccer when speaking to Americans, which causes confusion.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'foot-BALL'.

conversation.text: Are you watching football this Sunday?
We usually have people over to watch college football on Saturdays.
My son wants to play football, but I'm worried about injuries.

senses.definition: A low stool for supporting the feet while seated.
Anything trodden upon or treated as subservient.
senses.example: The scheming minister treated his rivals as a footstool for his ambitions, crushing them one by one.

core.definition: A low stool or padded support on which a seated person rests their feet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FUT. The second syllable rhymes with 'pool', so say 'stool' with a long 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and comfortable. It describes a household object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'footstool' for a small padded seat or ottoman placed in front of a chair or sofa. In modern American homes, many people say 'ottoman' for the same object, especially if it is upholstered and can hold a tray. A natural request is 'Can you put your feet up on the footstool?'

distinctions.note: An ottoman is often larger and upholstered, and may also serve as extra seating; a footstool is usually smaller and simpler.
A stool is a seat without a back; a footstool is for resting the feet, not for sitting on normally.

collocations: put your feet on a footstool

examples.everyday: Grandma always keeps a little footstool next to her armchair.
examples.professional: For the ergonomic review, we added a footstool to the standing desk setup.
examples.analytical: Psalm 110 describes God's enemies as a footstool, a picture of complete and humbling subjection.

nuance.analogy: A footstool is like a small landing for your feet: it lifts them slightly so you can relax fully.
nuance.etymology: From 'foot' and 'stool', literally a stool for the feet.
common_mistakes: Using 'footstool' for a bench or chair with a back; it is only for resting feet.
Confusing 'footstool' with 'footrest', which is usually a fixed bar or attachment.
nuance.biblical_note: Footstool is a symbol of authority and subjection in Scripture. Psalm 110:1 has the Lord say to the king, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool. Isaiah 66:1 says heaven is God's throne and the earth his footstool, and Matthew 5:35 echoes this image. The Hebrew word hadom means footstool, a symbol of royal dominion.

senses.definition: A person who forecasts.
A software program or algorithm that forecasts.

core.definition: A person, or a software program or model, that predicts future conditions or events, such as weather, sales or demand, from data and past patterns.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, FOR, and the word is not pronounced FOR-KAST-ur with equal weight. The stress stays on FOR in forecaster, but it moves to the second syllable in the verb forecast, which is fore-CAST in some speech, so keep the noun and verb patterns separate in your head.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes a role or tool without judgment, though a forecaster who is often wrong may be criticized for poor accuracy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forecaster most often for TV weather presenters, economists and analysts who publish predictions, and in data science for people or tools that predict demand or sales. In everyday talk, people usually say weather guy or meteorologist for a TV presenter, but forecaster is accepted and common. In technical settings, a time-series forecaster is a specific model type.

distinctions.note: A meteorologist is a trained scientist who studies the atmosphere, while a forecaster is anyone who makes a prediction, including a non-scientist or a model.
Predictor is the general term for any input variable in a model, while forecaster refers to the entity that produces forecasts over time.
A prophet claims divine or mystical insight, while a forecaster bases predictions on data and reasoning, so the two are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: Our local TV forecaster says it's going to snow Thursday, so I'm stocking up on milk tonight.
examples.professional: The demand forecaster on our team will update the model with last quarter's sales before Monday's planning meeting.
examples.analytical: A good forecaster is judged by calibration as well as accuracy, since a confident prediction that fails costs more than an honest range of possibilities.

nuance.analogy: A forecaster is like a navigator using dead reckoning: a confident estimate built from known data, corrected as new readings arrive.
nuance.etymology: From fore- 'before' + cast 'to calculate or throw', with the agent suffix -er marking the person or tool that does it.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (fore-CAST-er) instead of FOR-cast-er, which is typical of the verb form.
Using forecaster for a person who only guesses; Americans expect a forecaster to use data or a method, so a casual guess is a prediction, not a forecast.

senses.definition: An advance warning; an omen.

core.definition: A warning given in advance of something bad, or a sign that something unpleasant is likely to happen.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WOR, the second syllable. The r in both syllables is clearly pronounced in American speech, and the final -ing is a short, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral; it usually refers to a sign of trouble, though it can also refer to a neutral warning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forewarning in writing, in news, and in more formal speech, usually about a sign of danger or bad news. In everyday talk, people more often say warning or sign. You can say that was a forewarning or this was a forewarning of what was to come, and a natural reply is I should have listened.

distinctions.note: Warning is the general everyday word; forewarning stresses that it comes before the event and is often a sign of something to come.
An omen is a sign of a future event that may seem supernatural or mysterious; a forewarning can be a practical signal, such as a symptom.

examples.everyday: The dark clouds were a forewarning of the storm that hit right at lunch.
examples.professional: The spike in latency was a forewarning that the database would fail under the holiday load.
examples.analytical: Hume argues that past experience gives us no logical forewarning of what nature will do next.

nuance.analogy: A forewarning is like the yellow light before a red one: it gives you time to slow down before the danger arrives.
nuance.etymology: From fore- (before) and warning (a notice of danger), meaning a warning given beforehand.
common_mistakes: Using forewarning as a verb; the verb is forewarn, as in they forewarned us.
Writing forewarning with the wrong preposition, such as forewarning for danger; use forewarning of danger.

senses.definition: A penalty for or consequence of a misdemeanor.
senses.example: The court imposed a forfeit of two thousand dollars for the reckless violation.

senses.definition: A thing forfeited; that which is taken from somebody in requital of a misdeed committed; that which is lost, or the right to which is alienated, by a crime, breach of contract, etc.
senses.example: He who murders pays the forfeit of his own life.

senses.definition: Something deposited and redeemable by a sportive fine as part of a game.
senses.example: Each player put a silver coin in the pot as a forfeit before the game began.

senses.definition: Injury; wrong; mischief.
senses.example: Her cruel words wrought a forfeit upon the family that no apology could mend.

senses.definition: To suffer the loss of something by wrongdoing or non-compliance.
senses.example: He forfeited his last chance of an early release from jail by repeatedly attacking another inmate.

senses.definition: To lose a contest, game, match, or other form of competition by voluntary withdrawal, by failing to attend or participate, or by violation of the rules.
senses.example: Because only nine players were present, the football team was forced to forfeit the game.

senses.definition: To be guilty of a misdeed; to be criminal; to transgress.
senses.example: Those who forfeit the king's law shall answer for it before the assembly.

senses.definition: To fail to keep an obligation.
senses.example: Missing the delivery deadline means the supplier will forfeit the contract.

senses.definition: Of government officials: to legally remove property from its previous owners.
senses.example: The state may forfeit the property of anyone convicted of trafficking drugs.

senses.definition: Lost or alienated for an offense or crime; liable to penal seizure.
senses.example: The forfeit land reverted to the crown after the rebel lord was convicted of treason.

core.definition: To lose the right to something, or to lose something as a penalty for breaking a rule, failing to meet an obligation, or quitting a contest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FOR. The second syllable is short and reduced, sounding like 'fit'. The t at the end is clear, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies losing something important because of a mistake, rule violation, or choice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forfeit in sports, contracts, games, and legal situations. In casual conversation people often say 'give up' or 'lose' instead. In sports, a team that does not show up to a game can forfeit, and the result is recorded as a loss for them.

distinctions.note: Lose is general and everyday. Forfeit implies losing something as a consequence of a rule, penalty, or voluntary withdrawal.
Surrender means giving up in conflict or pressure. Forfeit usually refers to losing a right or game under a rule or contract.

examples.everyday: If we don't show up by seven, we'll forfeit our reservation, so let's leave now.
examples.professional: If the vendor misses the deadline, they forfeit the holdback payment under section four of the contract.
examples.analytical: Locke argues that a person who violates the natural law may forfeit certain rights, which raises the question of how such forfeiture can be justified without destroying the rights themselves.

nuance.analogy: Like a ticket that expires at the gate: once you break the rule, the thing you held is taken back.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'forfait', meaning a crime or transgression, from 'forfaire' meaning to transgress.
common_mistakes: Confusing forfeit with forgo, which means to go without something voluntarily, not to lose it as a penalty.
Pronouncing the final t as a flap, as in 'water', when it should be a clear t sound.

senses.definition: The mineralized remains of an animal or plant.
Any preserved evidence of ancient life, including shells, imprints, burrows, coprolites, and organically-produced chemicals.
senses.example: Paleontologists found a fossil of a trilobite, complete with its segmented shell, in the limestone quarry.

senses.definition: A fossil word.
senses.example: Hang up is a fossil from the days of physical telephones, still used today.

senses.definition: Anything extremely old, extinct, or outdated.
senses.example: Our office still runs on a fax machine, a fossil that nobody has bothered to replace.

senses.definition: An extremely old or outdated person.
senses.example: Grandpa calls himself a fossil when he refuses to learn how to use the smartphone.

senses.definition: A piece of media heavily promoted by a social media algorithm in spite of the media's old age.
senses.example: The algorithm keeps pushing a 2009 music video into my feed, a fossil I never asked to see.

core.definition: The preserved remains or traces of an ancient animal or plant, often turned to stone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced to a light uh, and the final l is syllabic, so it sounds like FAH-sull with almost no vowel between s and l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science; in casual speech it can be mildly negative when used as slang for an old-fashioned person or thing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fossil in everyday talk for real ancient remains, as in dinosaur fossils. Informally, people also call an outdated person or idea a fossil, which can sound a bit rude. Fossil fuel is a common phrase in energy and climate discussions.

distinctions.note: A relic is an old object kept for its history or value; a fossil is a preserved trace of ancient life, usually in rock.
An artifact is something made by people; a fossil is a natural remain of an ancient organism.

examples.everyday: We found a small shell fossil on the beach, and my kids were thrilled.
examples.professional: The geologist sent the fossil samples to the lab so they could be dated.
examples.analytical: The fossil record is incomplete, so paleontologists must infer evolutionary relationships from fragmentary remains.

nuance.analogy: Like a photo of a footprint in wet cement that hardened long ago: the trace survives after the living thing is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fossilis, 'dug up', from fodere, 'to dig'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable
Using fossil for living things that are merely old
Pronouncing the final l as a separate syllable with a full vowel

fossil.etymology: From French *fossile*, from Latin *fossilis* (“something which has been dug up”), from *fodio* (“to dig up”).

senses.definition: Any fuel derived from hydrocarbon deposits such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and, to some extent, peat; these fuels are non-renewable, and their burning moves carbon from underground into the atmosphere via the greenhouse gas carbon dioxide.
senses.example: Many climate scientists want countries to phase out fossil fuel use by the middle of the century.

core.definition: Fuel, such as coal, oil, or natural gas, formed from ancient buried organic matter that releases carbon dioxide when burned.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FYOO in fuel, and the first word is lighter. Do not pronounce the o in fossil as in 'boss'; it is a reduced vowel, so say 'FAH-suhl.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science and news, but often negative in climate debates.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fossil fuel constantly in news, politics, and everyday conversation about climate change and energy bills. The plural 'fossil fuels' is common when naming types. The usual contrast is with 'renewable energy' or 'clean energy,' such as solar and wind power.

distinctions.note: A fossil is any preserved remain of an ancient organism, while a fossil fuel is specifically a fuel made from such remains.
Fossil fuels are finite and release carbon when burned, while renewable energy comes from sources that are replenished, such as sunlight and wind.

examples.everyday: We drive less on weekends so we burn fewer fossil fuels.
examples.professional: Our data center still gets most of its electricity from fossil fuel plants, so our carbon footprint is high.
examples.analytical: The claim that fossil fuels remain necessary for economic growth depends on contested assumptions about how quickly alternatives can replace them.

nuance.analogy: Like a savings account that is drawn down but never refilled: once spent, the energy cannot be replaced on a human timescale.
nuance.etymology: Fossil comes from Latin fossilis, 'dug up'; fuel comes from Old French fouaille, from Latin focus, 'hearth.'
common_mistakes: Treating fossil fuel as a countable noun in general statements; use 'fossil fuels' when talking about several types.
Mispronouncing fossil with a strong second vowel, as in 'FOSS-eel.'

senses.definition: Covered with, or containing unclean matter; dirty.
senses.example: This cloth is too foul to use as a duster.

senses.definition: Obscene, vulgar or abusive.
senses.example: The rascal spewed forth a series of foul words.

senses.definition: Detestable, unpleasant, loathsome.
senses.example: He has a foul set of friends.

senses.definition: Disgusting, repulsive; causing disgust.
senses.example: This foul food is making me retch.

senses.definition: Unpleasant, stormy or rainy.
senses.example: Some foul weather is brewing.

senses.definition: Dishonest or not conforming to the established rules and customs of a game, conflict, test, etc.
senses.example: Foul play is not suspected.

senses.definition: (with "of") Positioned on, in, or near enough to (a specified area) so as to obstruct it.
senses.example: The anchored tanker lay foul of the shipping channel, blocking traffic for hours.

senses.definition: Entangled and therefore restricting free movement, not clear.
senses.example: We've got a foul anchor.

senses.definition: Outside of the base lines; in foul territory.
senses.example: Jones hit foul ball after foul ball.

senses.definition: To make dirty.
senses.example: to foul the face or hands with mire

senses.definition: To besmirch.
senses.example: He's fouled his reputation.

senses.definition: To obstruct, block, or otherwise interfere with (something), for example by clogging (a drain, gun barrel, chimney, etc) or by being in the way of (a gunshot, etc).
senses.example: The hair has fouled the drain.

senses.definition: To make a play, such as a strong contact with an opposing player in order to gain advantage, that is deemed by the referee to have contravened the rules.
senses.example: Smith fouled him hard.

senses.definition: To commit a foul.
senses.example: Smith fouled within the first minute of the quarter.

senses.definition: To become clogged.
senses.example: The drain fouled.

senses.definition: To become entangled.
senses.example: The prop fouled on the kelp.

senses.definition: To come into contact or collide with.
senses.example: The anchor chain fouled the propeller, so the boat drifted toward the rocks.

senses.definition: To entangle.
senses.example: The kelp has fouled the prop.

senses.definition: To hit outside of the baselines.
senses.example: Jones fouled the ball off the facing of the upper deck.

senses.definition: To hit a ball outside of the baselines.
senses.example: Jones fouled for strike one.

senses.definition: A (usually accidental) contact between a bowler and the lane before the bowler has released the ball.
