nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'heels' in casual conversation and 'high heels' when being more specific. The word 'heels' is almost always plural when talking about the shoes, as in 'a pair of high heels.' Pumps are closed-toe shoes that often have heels, while stilettos are very thin, high heels.

distinctions.note: Pumps are closed-toe, slip-on shoes that may or may not have a heel, while high heels are defined by the raised heel.
Stilettos are a specific style of very thin, very high heel, while high heels is a general term.
Wedges have a solid, sloped sole running from heel to toe instead of a separate raised heel.

examples.everyday: I can't walk in these high heels all night, so I'm changing into flats before we leave.
examples.professional: The conference venue has lots of marble floors, so you may want to skip the high heels.
examples.analytical: Historians trace high heels to riding footwear, and their meaning in Western fashion shifted over several centuries.

nuance.analogy: Like stilts for the foot: they change balance, posture, and how you walk.
nuance.etymology: From 'high' and 'heel,' describing shoes with a raised heel.
common_mistakes: Saying 'high heel' in the singular when talking about the shoes; the plural is standard.
Calling any shoe with a raised heel 'high heels'; boots with heels are usually called 'heeled boots' or 'boots with heels.'

senses.definition: In the tourist industry, the period of highest demand. In a sun and sand resort this means the hottest months, whereas in a ski resort, this means the coldest months.
senses.example: Hotel rates triple during high season, so we booked our ski trip early.

core.definition: The busiest and most expensive time of year for travel, hotels, or a resort, when demand and prices are highest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEE, the first syllable of 'season,' and the final syllable is a weak 'un.' Do not pronounce 'season' with two strong syllables, and keep the 'ee' long.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It signals higher prices and crowds rather than a positive or negative quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use high season mainly in travel, hotel, and resort talk, often with 'in high season' or 'during high season.' Peak season is a close synonym. Retail and tax professionals more often say 'busy season' or 'peak season,' so the term usually signals travel pricing.

distinctions.note: Peak season and high season both mean the busiest time, but high season is more common in travel pricing and resort marketing.
Shoulder season falls between the high and low seasons, with moderate prices and fewer crowds.
Low season is the quietest time with the lowest prices, while high season is the opposite.

examples.everyday: Hotels are way more expensive in high season, so we're going in October instead.
examples.professional: Our call center staffing has to cover the high season from late November through January.
examples.analytical: The economics of high season reveal how scarcity and price segmentation shape who can afford leisure travel.

nuance.analogy: Like rush hour on a highway: everything is busier, pricier, and more crowded.
nuance.etymology: From 'high' (at its greatest) and 'season' (a period of the year), used in travel and pricing contexts.
common_mistakes: Using 'high season' to describe hot or cold weather; it refers to demand and prices, not temperature.
Using 'high season' for every busy period at work; it is mainly for travel, resorts, and tourism.

senses.definition: A person or thing that hitchhikes.
An item attached to a travel bug and hidden in a geocache to be found and transported to other caches or around the world.
senses.example: She dropped the hitchhiker into a geocache in Oregon, then tracked its journey online.

senses.definition: A dance move in which the dancer mimics the motions of someone thumbing a ride.
senses.example: At the wedding party, my cousin showed off a hitchhiker that had everyone laughing.

senses.definition: An advertisement at the end of a program.
senses.example: The hitchhiker for the car dealership ran for thirty seconds after the late-night show.

senses.definition: A bur that attaches and clings to clothing, or a bur-bearing plant.
senses.example: The dog came home with a hitchhiker stuck in its fur after the trail walk.

core.definition: A person who travels by hitchhiking, standing by a road and asking drivers for a free ride.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HITCH, with a lighter secondary stress on 'hy'. The final '-er' is a quick American r-colored vowel, so say 'HITCH-hy-ker', not 'hitch-hyke-ur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can suggest adventure or vulnerability, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hitchhiker' for a traveler who gets rides from strangers, and it appears in films and books about the road. Many Americans advise against picking up hitchhikers because of safety concerns. The word is also known from 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy', a famous science fiction book and series.

distinctions.note: A passenger is any person riding in a vehicle, often by arrangement or payment; a hitchhiker is someone who asks strangers for the ride.
A pedestrian walks; a hitchhiker travels by asking drivers for rides.
A rider is someone who rides, often a planned companion; a hitchhiker is a stranger seeking an unplanned ride.

examples.everyday: We almost stopped for a hitchhiker on the highway, but my wife said no.
examples.professional: Our fleet policy forbids drivers to pick up hitchhikers, since the liability falls on the company.
examples.analytical: The lone hitchhiker in road films often stands for the outsider who must rely on the kindness of strangers.

nuance.analogy: A hitchhiker is like a stowaway who rides openly and asks permission first.
nuance.etymology: From 'hitchhike', a compound of 'hitch' and 'hike', with the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'hitch-HIKE-er'; the main stress is on HITCH.
Using 'hitchhiker' for someone who walks long distances; it refers specifically to getting rides.

senses.definition: Any of a family of sports in which hockey sticks are used to move a ball or puck into a goal.
senses.example: My daughter plays hockey on Saturday mornings, and I never miss her games.

senses.definition: Field hockey, a team sport played on a pitch on solid ground where players have to hit a ball into a net using a hockey stick.
senses.example: He helped his team beat the opponent at hockey 11-9 in a high-scoring match.

senses.definition: Ice hockey, a game on ice in which two teams of six players skate and try to score by shooting a puck into the opposing team's net, using their sticks.
senses.example: US stadiums are packed in the winter to see ice hockey.

senses.definition: Feces, excrement.
senses.example: The stable hadn't been cleaned, and the hockey piled up in the corners all week.

core.definition: A team sport played with sticks, usually meaning ice hockey in the United States, where players try to shoot a puck into the opposing team's net.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a light 'ee' sound. The 'o' is short, as in 'hot', not 'hoe'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is associated with sports fandom and, in northern states, with community and winter life.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, 'hockey' by itself almost always means ice hockey, played in the NHL and at colleges. If you mean the game played on grass with a ball, say 'field hockey'. Americans might ask 'Do you follow hockey?' in small talk, especially in northern cities.

distinctions.note: Field hockey is played on grass or turf with a ball; hockey alone usually means ice hockey in American speech.
Lacrosse uses a stick with a net pocket to catch and throw a ball; it is a different game from hockey.

examples.everyday: Are you going to the hockey game tonight? My son is finally on the team.
examples.professional: Our company sponsors a local hockey league, so a few of us are going to the game on Friday.
examples.analytical: Hockey culture in North America has often been linked to regional identity, especially in cold-weather communities.

nuance.analogy: Hockey on ice is like a fast, physical chess match on skates, where the puck moves quickly and every shot matters.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'hoquet', a shepherd's crook, which is related to the shape of the stick.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hockey' for field hockey without context, since Americans will assume ice hockey.
Pronouncing the first vowel as in 'hoe' rather than the short 'o' of 'hot'.

conversation.text: Hockey is huge in Minnesota and Canada.
I went to my first hockey game, and there was a fight on the ice.
My son plays hockey, so we're at the rink every weekend.

senses.definition: Dedicated to a religious purpose or a god.
senses.example: I'm planning to visit the holy city of Jerusalem this Christmas.

senses.definition: Revered in a religion.
senses.example: This tree is considered holy in my culture.

senses.definition: Morally perfect or flawless, or nearly so.
senses.example: My grandmother is a very holy woman.

senses.definition: Separated or set apart from (something unto something or someone else). (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The priests were holy to God, set apart from the people for temple service.

senses.definition: Set apart or dedicated for a specific purpose, or for use by a single entity or person.
senses.example: The monks kept this room holy, reserved only for prayer and quiet reflection.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier in various interjections.
senses.example: Holy cow, I can’t believe he actually lost the race!

senses.definition: An expression of astonishment and awe.
senses.example: Holy cow, you actually finished the marathon in under four hours!

core.definition: Dedicated or set apart for God or a religious purpose, and morally pure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: HOH-lee. The final -y is a long ee sound, like 'happy'. Do not say it as a long i as in 'high-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in religious contexts. In casual talk, holy is often used playfully, as in 'holy cow', and it can sound exaggerated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use holy most in religious settings, such as church, Bible study, and prayer, and in the phrase Holy Spirit. In everyday talk it is also an exclamation: 'holy cow' or 'holy smokes' show surprise. Calling something holy in casual speech can sound dramatic, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Sacred is more formal and often used about objects, places, and traditions, while holy describes the quality of God or a person set apart for God.
Pious describes outward religious devotion, while holy describes a deeper state of being set apart and pure.

examples.everyday: Holy cow, the line at the bakery is out the door this morning!
examples.professional: Our church leadership retreat focused on what it means to live a holy life in daily work.
examples.analytical: In Scripture, to call God holy is to affirm that God is set apart from creation in purity, majesty, and moral perfection.

nuance.analogy: Something holy is like a sealed vessel set aside for a special purpose, kept clean and reserved for its sacred use.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hālig, 'holy, sacred', related to whole and health.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long i, as in 'HOH-lye'.
Using holy to describe something merely special; in careful speech, reserve it for religious or morally pure things.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the key word is qadosh (set apart, holy), and in Greek it is hagios (holy, consecrated). Holiness belongs first to God, and things or people are holy when they are set apart for God. Leviticus 19:2 in the RSV tells Israel to be holy because the LORD their God is holy. Isaiah 6:3 shows the seraphim crying out that the LORD of hosts is holy. First Peter 1:15-16 applies this call to Christians, asking them to be holy in all their conduct.

holy.etymology: From Middle English *ali*, *aly*, *hale*, *halege*, *hali*, *halȝe*, *hayly*, *holi*, *holia*, *holie*, *holiȝ*, *holy*, *hooly*, *oli*, *oly*, *wholy*, *woly*, from Old English *hāleġ*, *hāliġ* (“holy, sacred; healthy, sound”), from **hailag*, from…

senses.definition: The manner in which a person conducts themselves at home, as opposed to how they act in a professional setting.
senses.example: Coworkers never saw his home life, which he kept completely separate from the office.

core.definition: The way a person lives and behaves at home, as distinct from how they act at work or in public.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIFE, with HOME only secondary. The vowel in home is a glide from oh toward oo, not a short hum, and the final f stays unvoiced, unlike the v in the verb live.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound positive or negative depending on context, as in 'a happy home life' or 'his home life is a mess'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase when talking about family, relationships and daily routines, especially in contrast with work. Asking 'How's your home life?' is personal, so save it for people you know well. It is common in casual talk, counseling and HR settings, and a natural reply is 'It's good, thanks' or 'It's been busy with the kids'.

distinctions.note: Private life covers all personal matters, including hobbies and friendships; home life focuses on family and the household.
Family life centers on relatives and their relationships; home life also covers your daily routines and how you act in your own house.

examples.everyday: My mom says my home life has been way calmer since I started running in the mornings.
examples.professional: Our benefits include flexible hours so employees can balance work and home life.
examples.analytical: Scholars of the family often examine how a person's home life shapes their identity beyond the workplace.

nuance.analogy: Like the back room of a store, where the real routines happen away from the shop floor.
nuance.etymology: Home comes from Old English ham, and life comes from Old English lif.
common_mistakes: Using home life to mean the building itself; say my house or my home for the place.
Pronouncing home with a short vowel like hum, which sounds unclear to American ears.

senses.definition: A short jump.
senses.example: The frog crossed the brook in three or four hops.

senses.definition: A jump on one leg.
A short journey, especially in the case of air travel, one that takes place on a private plane.
senses.example: We flew to Martha's Vineyard on a short hop in a friend's small private plane.

senses.definition: A brief period of development or progress.
senses.example: For popular radio stars in New York and Los Angeles, it was a short hop to network television.

senses.definition: A dance; a gathering for the purpose of dancing.
senses.example: The church hall was packed for the Saturday night hop, with a live swing band.

senses.definition: The sending of a data packet from one host to an adjacent host as part of its overall journey.
senses.example: The packet takes three hops through routers before reaching the destination server in Chicago.

senses.definition: A plant of species Humulus lupulus, native to northern Europe, female flowers of which are used to flavor many types of beer during brewing.
senses.example: Hops grown in the Pacific Northwest give this IPA its sharp, citrusy bitterness.

senses.definition: The flowers of the hop plant, dried and used to brew beer.
senses.example: The brewer weighed out a pound of dried hops for the next batch of pale ale.

senses.definition: Opium, or some other narcotic drug.
senses.example: Back in the 1890s, a dockside saloon in Boston sold hop to sailors who could not sleep.

senses.definition: The fruit of the dog rose; a hip.
senses.example: Along the hedgerow, the bright red hops of the wild dog rose glowed in October.

senses.definition: Synonym of half-op.
A bounce, especially from the ground, of a thrown or batted ball.
senses.example: The batter's grounder took a bad hop and struck him in the chin.

senses.definition: To jump a short distance.
senses.example: The kids hop over the puddle on their way to the bus stop.

senses.definition: To jump on one foot.
senses.example: Grandpa tried to hop on one leg while we counted to ten.

senses.definition: To be in state of energetic activity.
senses.example: Sorry, can't chat. Got to hop.

senses.definition: To suddenly take a mode of transportation that one does not drive oneself, often surreptitiously.
senses.example: I hopped a plane over here as soon as I heard the news.

senses.definition: To jump onto, or over.
senses.example: She hopped onto the kitchen counter to reach the top shelf.

senses.definition: To move frequently from one place or situation to another similar one.
senses.example: We were party-hopping all weekend.

senses.definition: To go in a quick or sudden manner.
senses.example: I'll hop over to the pharmacy and be back before dinner.

senses.definition: To dance.
senses.example: At the wedding, Grandma insisted on hopping with the grandkids to the polka music.

senses.definition: To impregnate with hops, especially to add hops as a flavoring agent during the production of beer.
senses.example: The brewery hops its pale ale heavily with Citra and Mosaic in the kettle.

senses.definition: To gather hops.
senses.example: Each September, migrant workers came to hop the fields outside Yakima.

core.definition: A short, quick jump, especially on one foot; also a short trip, especially by air.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short o of 'stop' and 'cot'. Americans pronounce it the same as 'hop' in cot-caught speech, so don't drift toward 'hope' or 'hup'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests something light, quick and easy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hop informally in everyday talk: hop on a plane, hop over to the store, or hop in the car. As a noun, a hop is usually a quick, short trip, such as a hop to Boston. Do not confuse it with hops, the beer plant, which is plural and pronounced with an s.

distinctions.note: A jump can be higher or use both feet; a hop is usually a short, light jump, often on one foot.
A skip is a step-and-hop movement with one foot after the other, while a hop uses one foot.
Hops are the flowers used to flavor beer; this plural noun is unrelated to the verb hop.

examples.everyday: I'll hop in the car and be there in ten minutes.
examples.professional: She hopped on a short flight to Chicago for the client meeting.
examples.analytical: Each logical hop in the argument needs an explicit premise, or the conclusion does not follow.

nuance.analogy: A hop is like a stone skipping on water: quick, light and off the surface for a moment.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hoppian, to leap.
common_mistakes: Using hop for a long-distance trip; a hop is short, so say flight or trip for a long journey.
Confusing hop with hope in speech because both begin with ho.

hop.etymology: From Middle English *hoppen*, from Old English *hoppian* (“to hop, spring, leap, dance”), from **huppōn*, from Proto-Germanic **huppōną* (“to hop”), from Proto-Indo-European **kewb-* (“to bend, bow”).

senses.definition: The art or science of cultivating gardens; gardening.
Small-scale agriculture.
senses.example: Her family's horticulture business supplied fresh vegetables to three farmers' markets across the county.

core.definition: The science and practice of growing fruits, vegetables, flowers, and ornamental plants in gardens or nurseries.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the final syllable a reduced American r-colored sound, not 'shur'. The middle 'ti' is a short 'tih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a professional or scientific field and sounds more formal than gardening.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use horticulture for the professional or scientific side of plant cultivation, such as a university horticulture program or a horticulture department at an extension office. For everyday talk about growing plants at home, people usually say gardening. Horticulturist is the usual word for the person.

distinctions.note: Gardening is the everyday activity of tending plants, while horticulture is the broader, more technical field of knowledge and practice.
Agriculture usually refers to large-scale farming of crops and livestock, while horticulture focuses on smaller-scale cultivation of garden and ornamental plants.

examples.everyday: My neighbor studied horticulture in college, so her backyard looks like a magazine photo.
examples.professional: Our landscaping firm hired two graduates with horticulture degrees to manage the client nurseries.
examples.analytical: Modern horticulture combines botany, soil chemistry, and ecology to explain how plants respond to their environment.

nuance.analogy: If gardening is cooking dinner at home, horticulture is the science of nutrition and food production behind the recipe.
nuance.etymology: From Latin hortus, garden, and cultura, cultivation.
common_mistakes: Confusing horticulture with agriculture when talking about small garden projects.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'shur' rather than a soft American 'chur'.

senses.definition: Collectively, products destined for use in the house, for example, for cleaning, cooking, eating, entertainment, personal hygiene, sleeping, and general upkeep.
senses.example: The moving company packed our household goods into a large truck on Monday.

core.definition: Personal possessions and items used inside a home, such as furniture, appliances, dishes and cleaning supplies.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GOODZ, and the final 'z' is voiced, like 'goods' with a buzz. Americans often say 'hows-hohld' quickly, with the second word of the compound slightly weaker.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical term used in business, moving and legal contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'household goods' most often in moving, shipping, insurance and retail. A moving company may ask about your household goods, and a store may have a household goods section. In casual talk people more often say 'stuff' or 'household things,' and 'household goods' sounds slightly formal or official.

distinctions.note: 'Household items' is more casual and used for individual objects, while 'household goods' sounds more formal or commercial and often refers to a category or collection.
Consumer goods is a broad economic category for anything sold to individuals, while household goods is narrower and focuses on items used inside the home.

examples.everyday: We need to sort out our household goods before the movers come on Saturday.
examples.professional: The procurement team placed a bulk order for household goods for the new apartment complex.
examples.analytical: Economists often track spending on household goods as an indicator of changes in domestic consumption.

nuance.analogy: Household goods are like the everyday tools in a workshop: each is small, but together they make the place function.
nuance.etymology: Household comes from Middle English houshold; goods comes from Old English gōd, property or possessions.
common_mistakes: Using 'household goods' for a single item; say 'a household item' or 'a piece of furniture' for one object.
Forgetting that 'goods' is plural, so the final consonant must be voiced as 'goodz.'

senses.definition: Asking how long someone has been in the area.

core.definition: Asking how many years someone has lived in the area or town.

pronunciation.respelling: how long hav yoo livd HEER
pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HERE, and 'lived' is pronounced 'livd' with a short i. Keep the r in 'here' clear, and reduce 'have you' to 'hav-yoo'.

nuance.connotation: Friendly and neutral; it shows interest in the person's history in the area.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this to neighbors, new coworkers and people they meet at community events. A natural reply is 'About six years. We moved from Ohio.' Avoid following up with pressing personal questions about the person's background, since small talk should stay light.

distinctions.vs: How long have you been here?
distinctions.note: Often refers to a shorter visit, work stint or temporary stay.
Asks about origin rather than length of residence.

collocations: how long have you lived here

examples.everyday: How long have you lived here? You seem to know everyone at the diner.
examples.professional: Welcome to the Austin team! How long have you lived here?
examples.analytical: Sociologists treat how long have you lived here as a rough measure of residential stability in neighborhood studies.

nuance.analogy: Like tree rings: the answer shows how deep someone's roots go in a place.
common_mistakes: Dropping the auxiliary and saying 'How long you live here?'
Using 'lived' with 'in' as in 'lived in here', which is not natural

conversation.text: "How long have you lived here?" "About five years now."
I love this neighborhood. How long have you lived here?
"How long have you lived here?" "My whole life, actually. I was born here."

senses.definition: The fundamental set of qualities, and the range of behavior, shared by (or believed by many to be shared by) all humans; the probabilities about thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that are typical among most humans.
senses.example: Some philosophers argue that there is fundamentally no such thing as human nature, but many people reject this thought for practical purposes because by human nature they merely mean predictable likelihoods about how humans can often be expected to think, feel, and behave.

core.definition: The characteristic qualities, feelings, and behavior shared by all people; in theology, what humans fundamentally are, including their created goodness and fallenness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NAY in 'nature'; 'human' has secondary stress on HYOO and a reduced 'mun'. The 't' in 'nature' sounds like 'ch', and the 'h' in 'human' is pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often used to excuse faults ('it's just human nature') or in solemn debate about good and evil.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in everyday speech to explain typical behavior. In philosophy, psychology and theology it is a technical subject. In Christology, 'human nature' refers to what Christ shares with us.

distinctions.note: Humanity can mean the human race or kindness; human nature is the shared character of people.
Personality is individual; human nature is universal.
The human condition is the circumstances of human life, like mortality; human nature is intrinsic qualities.
Anthropology is the study of humans; human nature is what is studied.

examples.everyday: People always put off taxes until the last minute; it's just human nature.
examples.professional: Good managers understand human nature and design incentives that reflect how people actually behave.
examples.analytical: Augustine and Pelagius disagreed about whether human nature, after the Fall, retains the power to choose the good unaided.

nuance.analogy: The factory settings every person comes with, whatever their culture.
nuance.etymology: From human, from Latin humanus, plus nature, from Latin natura, 'birth, character'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the human nature' when speaking generally; no article is normal.
Mispronouncing 'nature' as 'NAH-toor'.
Confusing it with 'humanity' meaning kindness.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture teaches humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:26-27) and are also fallen (Romans 5:12). Psalm 8:3-5 marvels at human dignity. Hebrew nephesh ('living being') and Greek sarx ('flesh') and psyche ('soul') figure in biblical anthropology, and Hebrews 2:14-17 says Christ shared in flesh and blood.

traditions.view: Human nature is created good in God's image and wounded by ancestral sin, which brought mortality and corruption but not inherited guilt. Salvation is healing and deification (theosis).
Nature is good but wounded by original sin, losing preternatural gifts and sanctifying grace; grace perfects nature rather than destroying it.

Reformers such as Luther and Calvin stressed total depravity: nature is corrupted in every part, though still bearing God's image. Arminian and Wesleyan groups emphasize prevenient grace enabling response.

senses.definition: The inclusion of hyphens; especially, the correct locations of hyphens.
senses.example: Print the article without hyphenation if you're not sure where to put them.

core.definition: The correct placement of hyphens in words, including where a word is split at the end of a line.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAY. The ending -tion is pronounced 'shun', with no strong vowel, so do not say 'shun' with a full UH-sound or stress it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used in editing and writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in editing, publishing, typography and software settings, such as 'automatic hyphenation' in a word processor. Most people in conversation would just say 'where the hyphens go' or 'how to hyphenate.' In an office, you might hear it when someone is discussing the layout of a document.

distinctions.note: A hyphen is the mark itself, while hyphenation is the process or set of rules for using it.
Syllabification is about dividing a word into sounds, but hyphenation is about where a line break or a compound joint is marked in writing.

examples.everyday: My sister's friend keeps asking about the hyphenation of her name on the wedding invitation.
examples.professional: We need to turn on automatic hyphenation in the report template so the justified text looks even.
examples.analytical: Hyphenation in English is governed by convention rather than by a single consistent logic, which is why style guides disagree.

nuance.analogy: Hyphenation is like the traffic signs on a road that show where to split the lane, not the road itself.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin hyphenatio, from Greek hyphen 'under one', meaning 'together as one'.
common_mistakes: Using 'hyphenation' to mean the mark itself, when the mark is simply a hyphen.
Stressing the -tion ending, which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: A set of specified or traditional symbolic forms associated with the subject or theme of a stylized genre of art.
senses.example: The church's iconography shows Saint Michael with a sword and scales.

senses.definition: The art of representation by pictures or images; the description or study of portraiture or representation, as of persons.
senses.example: the iconography of the ancients

senses.definition: The study of representative art in general.
senses.example: She took a seminar in iconography before writing her dissertation on Byzantine manuscripts.

core.definition: The traditional symbols, images and conventions used to represent a particular person, subject or theme in art.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'nah', the third syllable. The middle 'uh' is reduced, and the word ends with 'fee'. In American speech, the 'r' in 'gra' is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is precise vocabulary for art history and religious studies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'iconography' mainly in art history, museum studies, theology and cultural analysis. In everyday speech, people might say 'images' or 'symbols,' but 'iconography' is the right term when discussing traditional visual conventions. It can also describe the visual symbols in a logo or design brand.

distinctions.note: Imagery is a broader term for pictures or descriptive images in art or writing, while iconography refers to the established symbolic system of a tradition.
Symbolism is the use of symbols in general, while iconography is the study or set of specific traditional visual forms.

examples.everyday: The museum guide explained the iconography of the old painting, like why the saint holds a book.
examples.professional: Our brand team reviewed the iconography of the logo to make sure it reads clearly across regions.
examples.analytical: Medieval Christian iconography encoded theological claims, so a halo, a gesture or a color could communicate doctrine to viewers who could not read.

nuance.analogy: Iconography is like a visual dictionary: each symbol carries a fixed meaning that viewers learn to read.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'eikōn' (image) and '-graphia' (writing, description).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress falls on 'nah', not on 'ICK'.
Using 'iconography' to mean any picture, when it refers to a specific set of traditional symbols.

senses.definition: In an idolatrous manner.

core.definition: In a way that worships a false god or adores a person or thing excessively, as if it were a god.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, DAH, and the rest of the word is quick and unstressed. The ending -ous becomes a reduced 'uh-s', so say 'truh-slee', not 'trus-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies misplaced devotion, usually harshly judged.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in religious, literary, or critical writing and in serious sermons or commentary. In everyday speech it sounds heavy, so people would more likely say 'worship' or 'obsess over' something. A natural reply to a claim like this is 'That's strong, but I see what you mean.'

distinctions.note: Devoutly means with sincere, faithful religious devotion, while idolatrously means devotion that has been directed to a false object.
Idolize is an everyday verb for admiring someone intensely, while idolatrously is a formal adverb with a strong religious charge.

examples.everyday: He talks about his old truck as if it were a god, and honestly, he treats it idolatrously.
examples.professional: Our leadership treats every quarterly metric idolatrously, so nobody questions whether the numbers measure anything useful.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that modern consumers relate to brands idolatrously, giving them a loyalty that properly belongs only to what is true and good.

nuance.analogy: Like a fan who treats a celebrity's every word as scripture.
nuance.etymology: From idolatrous, from Greek eidōlolatrēs, 'image-worshiper', from eidōlon 'image' and latreuein 'to serve'.
common_mistakes: Using idolatrously as an adjective; the adjective is idolatrous.
Using it for mild admiration; it implies excessive or misplaced devotion.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the central terms are the Hebrew pesel, a carved image, and the Greek eidōlon, an image or idol; the act is called eidōlolatreia in Greek, 'image-worship'. Exodus 20:4-5 forbids making carved images to bow down to them. Galatians 5:20 lists idolatry among the works of the flesh. 1 John 5:21 ends with a warning to keep yourselves from idols.

traditions.view: Icons are venerated, not worshiped; the honor shown to an icon passes to the person it depicts, a distinction affirmed by the Seventh Ecumenical Council in 787, so veneration is not idolatry.

Catholics distinguish latria, the worship owed to God alone, from dulia and hyperdulia, the honor given to saints and Mary, so honoring sacred images is not idolatry when the honor is directed to the one depicted.

Many Protestants, especially Reformed, some Baptist and some Pentecostal groups, regard religious images in worship as a danger of idolatry and reject them, while Lutherans and Anglicans have been more tolerant of images as teaching aids, though both condemn trust placed in them.

core.definition: An ancient region south of Judah, settled by the Edomites, descendants of Esau, and later brought under Jewish control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEE, the third syllable. Say the first two syllables quickly, with the y sound before oo, and end on a clear uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and geographical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Idumaea mainly in Bible study, church history or discussions of Herod the Great, whose family came from there. It is not used as a common noun, and the adjective is Idumaean. Say ID-yoo-MEE-uh; in Hebrew the same land is called Edom.

distinctions.note: Edom is the Hebrew name for the same region and people, while Idumaea is the Greek and Roman name, used especially for the later period.
Judea lay north of Idumaea, and in the Roman period the two were often administered together.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent a while on Herod last week, and someone pointed out that his family came from Idumaea.
examples.professional: For the history unit in our curriculum, I need a map showing Idumaea just south of Judea.
examples.analytical: The Hasmonean conquest of Idumaea and the forced conversion of its people shaped the political identity of the Herodian dynasty.

nuance.analogy: Like a border district that changes hands so often that its residents keep having to learn a new name for their home.
nuance.etymology: Latinized from Greek Idoumaia, from Hebrew Edom, meaning red, the name given to Esau in Genesis.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with Judea or Israel
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in id-YOO-mee-uh
Using it as a common noun for any desert region
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 25:30 Esau is given the name Edom, meaning red, and Genesis 36:1 identifies Esau with Edom, so the region and its people descend from him. Mark 3:8 lists people from Idumea among those who came to Jesus, showing how far his fame had spread. Herod the Great, whose family was Idumaean, ruled Judea under Roman authority, and many Jews resented a king of Edomite descent.

senses.definition: Not approved by law, but not invalid.
senses.example: The bigamous marriage, while illicit, was not invalid.

senses.definition: Breaking social norms.
senses.example: The teenagers kept their illicit romance secret from both sets of strict parents.

senses.definition: Unlawful.
senses.example: Police raided the warehouse, seizing illicit fireworks and several crates of counterfeit medicine.

senses.definition: A banned or unlawful item.
senses.example: Customs agents found illicits hidden inside the spare tire of the delivery van.

core.definition: Not allowed by law or by accepted social rules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, LIS. The final 't' is a clear, light 't', not a flap, and the first syllable is a weak 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests wrongdoing, secrecy or something prohibited, and is stronger than 'unusual'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'illicit' for illegal goods, activities or behavior, such as 'illicit drugs' or 'illicit trade'. In everyday speech people often say 'illegal' for crimes; 'illicit' sounds more formal and suggests something hidden or morally questionable. It is common in news, law and policy writing.

distinctions.note: 'Illegal' means against the law; 'illicit' can also mean breaking social rules or being immoral, and it often implies secrecy.
'Unlawful' is a formal legal term; 'illicit' is broader and more common in news and everyday discussion of trade or relationships.

examples.everyday: The cops found some illicit fireworks in the trunk, so the guy got arrested.
examples.professional: Our security team flagged illicit access attempts from an unknown IP address last night.
examples.analytical: Rawls distinguishes lawful protest from illicit force, asking when disobedience is justified.

nuance.analogy: An illicit act is like a door marked 'Staff Only' that someone walks through anyway; it's a line that shouldn't be crossed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'illicitus', from 'in-' (not) plus 'licitus' (permitted).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'ih-LYE-sit', with the wrong vowel.
Using 'illicit' for mere unusual behavior; it implies wrongdoing.

illicit.etymology: French *illicite*, from Latin *illicitus*, from *in-* (“not”) + *licitus* (“allowed, permitted”), from *licet* (“it is allowed”).

senses.definition: In an illustrative manner.

core.definition: In a way that serves as an example or makes an idea clearer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root, LUHS. The ending -ively is often said as -iv-lee, with the vowel in -ive reduced; avoid stressing the -tive part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds scholarly and precise, so it fits writing more than speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in casual conversation. It appears in academic writing, technical manuals, and formal reports, where a writer says a point is presented illustratively. In speech, Americans usually say 'as an example' or 'to show what I mean.'

distinctions.note: For example is the natural spoken phrase; illustratively is a formal adverb for describing the manner of a presentation.

examples.everyday: The hiking guide explained the trail signs illustratively, with a drawing of each one.
examples.professional: The report presents the three scenarios illustratively, so the board can compare the outcomes quickly.
examples.analytical: Plato uses the cave image illustratively, not as a complete account of knowledge but as a way to show its stages.

nuance.analogy: If an explanation is a map, illustratively describes how the map is drawn: with examples that point to the real terrain.
nuance.etymology: Formed from illustrative with the adverb ending -ly, from Latin illustrare, to make clear.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as ih-luh-STRAY-tiv-lee.
Using it in casual speech where for example sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Experiencing an imbalance; out of balance.
senses.example: The dataset is heavily imbalanced, with only two percent of transactions labeled as fraud.

core.definition: Not evenly proportioned; having too much of one thing and too little of another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on BAL. The ending -anced is a single soft syllable, so say 'unst' without adding a separate 'ced' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral: it describes a problem or an unfair state; in data science it is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: 'Imbalanced dataset' is the standard phrase in data science. In everyday talk Americans use it for diets, teams, or news coverage: 'the coverage was imbalanced.' Calling a person imbalanced can sound like a psychological judgment, so avoid it for people.

distinctions.note: Unbalanced is the more common everyday word and can mean mentally unstable in some contexts; imbalanced is more neutral and often technical.
Biased suggests a deliberate or systematic tilt toward a view; imbalanced describes proportions in the data or situation without judging intent.

examples.everyday: My diet has been pretty imbalanced lately, so I'm eating more vegetables.
examples.professional: Our fraud model has good accuracy but poor recall, because the training data is heavily imbalanced.
examples.analytical: A debate that is heavily imbalanced in speaking time cannot really be called deliberative, whatever its participants intend.

nuance.analogy: An imbalanced dataset is like a choir where one section sings forty times louder: you hear mostly that part.
nuance.etymology: From im- 'not' plus balanced, the past participle of balance.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable and saying 'im-buh-LANST'; the stress is on BAL.
Using imbalanced as a noun; say 'an imbalance' for the noun form.

senses.definition: To overlap in a regular pattern.
To undergo or cause to undergo imbrication.
senses.example: The roofers imbricate the cedar shingles so each row overlaps the one below.

core.definition: To arrange or overlap in a regular, shingle-like pattern, with each part partly covering the next.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, IM. The middle vowel is a reduced 'ih', and the final -ate is pronounced 'ayt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: Mainly used in biology, geology, architecture, and botany to describe scales, tiles, or sediment layers. Americans would say 'overlap' or 'shingled' in everyday speech. Use it in technical writing; it sounds precious in conversation.

distinctions.note: Overlap is general and everyday; imbricate describes a regular pattern in which each piece partly covers the next, like roof shingles.
Tile is a noun for a flat covering; imbricate is the verb for how such pieces are arranged.

examples.everyday: The pinecone's scales imbricate so tightly that rain can barely get in.
examples.professional: The drainage layer imbricates the stones so that water flows off without washing out the soil.
examples.analytical: In medieval stonework, imbricated courses kept water from seeping through the joints, and the pattern became a visual emblem of order.

nuance.analogy: Imbricated pieces are like fish scales or roof shingles, each one overlapping the one below it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imbricare 'to cover with tiles', from imbrex 'roof tile'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with imbue or imbibe; the pronunciation is IM-brih-kayt.
Using it in everyday speech where overlap is clearer.

senses.definition: The act of imperiling, or the state of being imperiled.

core.definition: The act of putting something or someone in danger, or the state of being in danger.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEHR, the second syllable, and the r is clear. The ending -ment is weak, so say it as 'muhnt' rather than a full 'ment'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes harm or danger to people, property, or the environment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use imperilment in formal writing, environmental reports, or literary discussions. Peril and endangerment are more common in everyday speech. You will hear imperil more often as a verb than imperilment as a noun.

distinctions.note: Peril is the usual everyday noun for danger, while imperilment is a formal noun for the act of putting something at risk.
Endangerment is common in environmental and legal writing, while imperilment is more literary and less frequent.

examples.everyday: The storm caused real imperilment for families living near the river, so the town opened a shelter.
examples.professional: The risk review identifies the imperilment of key data systems as the main concern for the next release.
examples.analytical: Augustine's argument about the imperilment of the soul by pride treats sin as a danger that threatens a person's whole relationship with God.

nuance.analogy: Imperilment is like a bridge with a cracked support beam: the structure still stands, but every load on it now carries a hidden risk.
nuance.etymology: From imperil, from Old French empereillier, from en- plus peril, danger, plus the English noun ending -ment.
common_mistakes: Using imperilment when peril is more natural in everyday talk, as in 'in great imperilment' instead of 'in great peril'.
Confusing imperil, the verb meaning to endanger, with imperial or imperialism.

senses.definition: In a way or to an extent that is not permissible.
senses.example: The judge ruled that the prosecutor had impermissibly questioned the witness about her prior record.

core.definition: In a way that is not allowed by rules, law, policy or moral standards.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MIS, as in the adjective. The final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound, and the -ible part reduces to 'ih-bul' before it.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes an action carried out in a way that breaks a rule or standard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb mainly in legal, academic, technical and compliance writing, often in phrases like 'obtained impermissibly' or 'used impermissibly'. In casual speech they say 'the wrong way' or 'not allowed'. The word is rare in conversation, so it sounds formal.

distinctions.note: Illegally specifically means breaking the law; impermissibly covers any violation of an allowed standard.
Improperly is the more everyday word for doing something the wrong way; impermissibly is stronger and more formal.

examples.everyday: The driver had parked impermissibly close to the fire hydrant, so he got a ticket.
examples.professional: The team had used the sample impermissibly, so the results were removed from the final report.
examples.analytical: The court held that the evidence had been obtained impermissibly and could not be used at trial.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner stepping over the line in a race, where the rules say that a step is not allowed.
nuance.etymology: Formed from impermissible plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin in- 'not' and permittere 'allow'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adverb with the adjective; say 'acted impermissibly', not 'acted impermissible'.
Stressing the first syllable and saying 'IM-per-mis-ib-ly'.

senses.definition: A self-referencing definition.
senses.example: In type theory, the logic's impredicativity allows a proposition to quantify over all propositions, including itself.

core.definition: The property of a definition or set that quantifies over a totality containing the very object being defined, a source of paradox in logic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TIV, and the -ity ending is a reduced 'uh-tee'. The adjective impredicative stresses PRED instead, so the stress shifts in the noun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in logic, set theory, and the philosophy of mathematics, often when discussing Russell's paradox or foundations of mathematics. In everyday talk people say 'circular' instead, and the technical term sounds stiff outside a seminar or paper. Mathematicians often contrast it with predicativity.

distinctions.note: Circularity is any self-dependent reasoning; impredicativity is a narrower technical property about quantifying over a totality that includes the defined object.
Predicative definitions quantify only over objects defined earlier, so impredicativity is the opposite property rather than a synonym.

examples.everyday: Honestly, my logic professor lost me when she started going on about impredicativity.
examples.professional: Before we submit, reviewers will ask whether the construction is impredicative, since that would undermine our induction argument.
examples.analytical: Russell's objection turns on whether a definition's impredicativity, its reference to a totality containing the defined object, is itself vicious.

nuance.analogy: Like defining a club by its members when one member is the club itself: the definition needs the whole that includes what it defines.
nuance.etymology: From im- 'not' plus predicative, from Latin praedicare 'to declare'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual synonym for 'circular', which sounds technical and can confuse listeners.
Keeping the stress on PRED as in the adjective impredicative; in the noun the stress shifts to TIV.

senses.definition: Being easily influenced (especially of young people).
An impressionable person.
senses.example: Advertisers often target the impressionable, especially children who cannot yet judge claims critically.

core.definition: Easily influenced by others, new ideas, or experiences, especially when young or inexperienced.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PRESH, and the 'sion' ending is pronounced 'shun.' The last syllables are reduced, so say 'nuh-bul' rather than 'nuh-bull' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Often mildly negative when it describes children or vulnerable people being exposed to bad influences; neutral when describing openness to learning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this word when talking about children, teenagers, or media influence, as in 'Kids are impressionable, so be careful what they watch.' It can sound a bit formal or judgmental, so in casual talk people often say 'easily influenced.'

distinctions.note: Susceptible means likely to be affected by something harmful, like illness or manipulation; impressionable focuses on being shaped by influence, especially in youth.
Gullible means too ready to believe what you are told; impressionable describes being shaped by experience and influence, not necessarily being fooled.

examples.everyday: Be careful what you say around the kids, because they're really impressionable at that age.
examples.professional: Our marketing campaign should avoid messages that could mislead impressionable younger users who are new to the platform.
examples.analytical: Plato worried that impressionable citizens, especially the young, would absorb poetry's images without judging their truth.

nuance.analogy: An impressionable mind is like wet clay: it takes the shape of whatever presses on it.
nuance.etymology: From impression plus the suffix -able, meaning capable of being impressed.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as im-pre-SHUN-uh-bul.
Confusing it with 'impressive,' which describes something that causes admiration.

senses.definition: A confinement in a place, especially a prison or a jail, especially as punishment for a crime.

core.definition: The state of being confined in a prison or jail, usually as punishment for a crime; the period of such confinement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PRIZ, and the middle syllable is reduced to 'un.' The ending 'ment' is a short, weak syllable, not 'mint' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it refers to punishment or confinement and often appears in legal and news contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use imprisonment in courts, news reports, and legal discussions, as in 'a sentence of ten years' imprisonment.' In everyday speech, people usually say 'time in prison' or 'jail time.' The word can also describe unlawful confinement, as in 'false imprisonment.'

distinctions.note: Incarceration is a more formal and often policy-focused term for the system of confinement; imprisonment usually refers to a particular punishment or period.
Custody means legal control or temporary holding, which may not involve punishment; imprisonment usually refers to confinement after conviction.

examples.everyday: My uncle was facing a year of imprisonment, but the judge gave him probation instead.
examples.professional: The legal team warned that the fraud charges could bring up to five years of imprisonment, so we need to review our exposure.
examples.analytical: Augustine asks whether earthly imprisonment can truly limit the soul, and his answer distinguishes bodily confinement from inner freedom.

nuance.analogy: Imprisonment is like a locked room with no key: the person cannot leave until the sentence or the lock is removed.
nuance.etymology: From imprison plus the suffix -ment, forming a noun for a state or action.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable or saying 'im-pree-ZON-ment' with a wrong vowel.
Using it for a short stay in a holding cell; in everyday American speech, 'detention' or 'custody' may be more accurate.

senses.definition: In fact; in truth.

core.definition: In fact, as things really are, in contrast with how they seem, are described, or are assumed to be.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AL, the third syllable of actuality, with a lighter secondary stress on ak. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable, as in ACT-choo-al-i-tee, which sounds unnatural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it contrasts reality with appearance and can sound corrective, especially in argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in writing, speeches, and analysis to set reality against an appearance or claim: 'It looked like a quick fix, but in actuality it took months.' In casual speech they say 'actually' or 'in fact.' A natural reply is 'Oh, I didn't realize that.'

distinctions.note: Everyday and flexible, used to correct or emphasize; 'in actuality' is more formal and sets reality against appearance.
Nearly identical in meaning, and more common in everyday American speech.
More neutral and conversational, often adding a supporting detail rather than contrasting with an appearance.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says he fixed the fence himself, but in actuality his brother did most of it.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows full uptime, but in actuality the service failed twice last week.
examples.analytical: The text presents an ideal of equality, yet in actuality it protects only property owners.

nuance.analogy: Like the map and the territory: the map may look complete, but the land it shows is what counts.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin actualitas, meaning reality, from Latin actualis, meaning active or real.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as ACT-choo-al-i-tee
Using it in casual talk where 'actually' or 'in fact' sounds more natural

senses.definition: Resulting from the actions of parties.
senses.example: The contract was breached in fact when the vendor delivered nothing at all.

senses.definition: Actually; in truth; de facto.
senses.example: People think he's rich, but in fact he's nearly penniless.

senses.definition: Moreover.
senses.example: I don't have the time or patience to deal with him. In fact, I barely even have time for being here at all.

core.definition: Actually; really; as a true fact, often used to add or correct information.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -FACT, and the 'in' is weak. Link the two words smoothly so it sounds like one phrase, and let the final t be a quick stop.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals a clarification, a correction or emphasis. Used sharply, it can sound like a contradiction, as in 'In fact, you're wrong.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to add a surprising or important detail, as in 'I thought the store closed at six, but in fact it's open until nine.' It is common in everyday and professional talk and writing. In speech, it often comes with a slight pause before 'in fact', and the stress usually falls on 'fact'.

distinctions.note: Actually is more common in everyday speech and often signals surprise or contrast, while in fact is slightly more formal and emphasizes a verified point.
Indeed is formal and used to confirm or intensify what was just said, while in fact adds new information or corrects a belief.

examples.everyday: I thought the coffee shop closed at six, but in fact it stays open until nine.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows a drop in conversions, but in fact the drop came from a tracking bug we introduced last week.
examples.analytical: Hume's skepticism suggests that causation is not in fact observed but only inferred from constant conjunction.

nuance.analogy: Like lifting a rug to find what was hiding underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Latin in facto, 'in the deed', from factum, 'something done'.
common_mistakes: Using 'in fact' to start almost every sentence, which sounds stiff and repetitive in casual talk.
Confusing 'in fact' with 'the fact is', which is more natural when introducing a single key point.

in-fact.etymology: From *fact* (“deed, action”) now obsolete, except in law.

senses.definition: In fashion.
senses.example: Disco went out of style in the 1980s, but is now in style again.

senses.definition: With flair.
senses.example: She's so elegant, no matter what she does, she does it in style.

core.definition: In fashion; popular and current in clothing, decor or taste. Also, done with flair and elegance.

pronunciation.tip: 'Style' is one syllable with a long 'i' sound, so don't add an extra syllable like 'styl-uh'. The word 'in' is unstressed and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is complimentary when describing appearance or manner, though it can be a bit superficial when describing trends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'in style' mostly for clothes, home decor, cars or events: 'Wide-leg jeans are really in style again.' It also appears in 'do something in style', meaning with flair, as in 'She threw a party in style.' The opposite, 'out of style', is equally common. A natural reply is 'Yeah, they really are.'

distinctions.note: 'In fashion' focuses on what is trendy at the moment; 'in style' can also mean doing something with flair.
'Stylish' describes a person or thing with good taste; 'in style' describes what is current or done with flair.
'In vogue' is more formal and slightly literary, while 'in style' is everyday American English.

examples.everyday: Those wide-leg pants are really in style right now, so you made a good choice.
examples.professional: The new dashboard uses a flat design that is very in style, but our users need clarity more than trends.
examples.analytical: Postmodern architecture was in style for a time, yet its popularity owed as much to fashion as to any considered theory of form.

nuance.analogy: Like a song everyone is humming this month: it's the sound of the moment, and it will fade.
nuance.etymology: 'Style' from Latin stilus, a pointed writing tool, through Old French and Middle English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in the style' for the general fashionable sense; the fixed phrase is 'in style'.
Using 'in style' for every kind of fashion talk; in some contexts 'in fashion' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Recently started but not fully formed yet; just begun; only elementary or immature.
senses.example: The startup's business plan was still inchoate, with only a rough sketch of the product.

senses.definition: Chaotic, disordered, confused; also, incoherent, rambling.
senses.example: His rambling, inchoate email about the project left the team completely confused.

senses.definition: Of a crime, imposing criminal liability for an incompleted act.
senses.example: The prosecutors charged him with an inchoate offense, conspiracy to commit fraud, even though no money changed hands.

senses.definition: To begin or start (something).
senses.example: The committee will inchoate the reforms next semester, beginning with a pilot program.

senses.definition: To cause or bring about. In the field of criminology, to encourage, assist, conspire, aid and abet, incite, etc.
senses.example: The ringleader inchoated the riot by spreading rumors among the crowd outside the factory.

senses.definition: To make a start.
senses.example: The team started to inchoate on the draft before the funding was finally approved.

senses.definition: (rare) A beginning, an immature start.
senses.example: Historians trace the movement's inchoate to a small meeting in a church basement.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Just begun and not yet fully formed, organized, or developed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOH. The ch is pronounced as k, and the ending is a reduced it, not 'eight'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes something unfinished in an abstract way, sometimes slightly critical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inchoate mostly in writing, essays, and academic or literary discussion, for ideas, plans, or feelings that are still vague. In speech it sounds stiff or pretentious. In everyday talk say vague, unformed, or just getting started.

distinctions.note: Embryonic suggests early growth with clear potential; inchoate suggests disorganization or lack of shape.
Nascent is more common and usually positive, describing something newly emerging.

examples.everyday: I had an inchoate sense that something was wrong, but I couldn't put a name to it.
examples.professional: The proposal is still inchoate, so we need a working group to shape the requirements.
examples.analytical: Early Hegelian sketches of freedom remain inchoate until they are worked out in the later systematic writings.

nuance.analogy: Like a pencil sketch before the painting is finished, an inchoate idea has its outline but not its substance.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inchoatus, past participle of inchoare 'to begin'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch as in chair; it is pronounced as k.
Using it for a finished but simple thing; it means not yet formed.

inchoate.etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb circa 1631; Latin *incohātus* (“begun, unfinished”), perfect passive participle of *incohō* (“to begin”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: The doctrine that free will and determinism are incompatible, that one necessarily precludes the other.

core.definition: The philosophical view that free will and determinism cannot both be true, so one excludes the other.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL, the fourth syllable, and the final -ism is a reduced um. Do not stress the first syllable, and say the vowel in -pat- clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use incompatibilism almost only in philosophy classes, papers and debates about free will. In everyday talk one would say 'I don't think free will fits with determinism'. It is a precise label, so using it in casual conversation may sound overly academic.

distinctions.note: Compatibilism holds that free will and determinism can both be true, while incompatibilism holds that they cannot.
Libertarianism in this sense is a form of incompatibilism that affirms free will and denies determinism, whereas incompatibilism alone only says the two cannot coexist.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure about free will, but I tend toward a kind of incompatibilism where determinism would rule it out.
examples.professional: In the ethics seminar, we discussed whether incompatibilism or compatibilism better explains our intuitions about responsibility.
examples.analytical: Incompatibilism claims that if determinism is true, no one could have done otherwise, so moral responsibility would be impossible.

nuance.analogy: Like two rules for a game that cannot both be followed at once: if one holds, the other must fail.
nuance.etymology: From in- 'not' plus compatibilism, from Latin compatibilis 'able to exist together', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing incompatibilism with compatibilism and reversing the meaning.
Stressing the first syllable instead of BIL.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to or supporting incompatibilism.
senses.example: Her incompatibilist view holds that free will cannot coexist with a fully determined universe.

senses.definition: A proponent of incompatibilism.
senses.example: In our seminar, the incompatibilist argued that determinism rules out moral responsibility entirely.

core.definition: A philosopher who holds that free will and determinism cannot both be true, so one must be rejected.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'BIL', the fourth syllable, and the ending '-ist' is a short 'ist'. Do not stress 'pat' as strongly as 'BIL', and reduce the vowels in 'in-kuhm' to quick schwas.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term in philosophy and carries no judgment about whether the position is right.
nuance.usage_note: This term is used almost only in philosophy, especially in debates about free will and moral responsibility. Ordinary Americans would say that someone 'doesn't believe in free will' or is a 'determinist'. You will hear it in university classes, academic talks, and philosophy papers.

distinctions.note: A compatibilist holds that free will and determinism can both be true, while an incompatibilist denies that they can.
A hard determinist is an incompatibilist who accepts determinism and therefore denies free will; an incompatibilist can also be a libertarian who accepts free will.
A libertarian in this sense accepts free will and rejects determinism, while the term incompatibilist only says the two cannot be true together.

examples.everyday: My roommate is an incompatibilist, so he says we can't really choose anything if the universe is fully determined.
examples.professional: In the AI ethics review, one incompatibilist member argued that predictive models should never be treated as morally responsible agents.
examples.analytical: The incompatibilist insists that if every event is fixed by prior causes, then no agent could have done otherwise in any morally relevant sense.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who insists that a game with a fixed outcome cannot also be a fair contest.
nuance.etymology: From incompatible, from Medieval Latin incompatibilis, with the suffix -ist; the philosophical sense developed in the twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'incompatibilist' (a person who holds a view) with 'incompatibility' (a conflict between things).
Using it casually for people who simply do not get along; in philosophy it refers only to free will and determinism.

senses.definition: To include (something) as a part.
senses.example: The design of his house incorporates a spiral staircase.

senses.definition: To mix (something in) as an ingredient; to blend.
senses.example: Incorporate air into the mixture by whisking.

senses.definition: To admit as a member of a company.
senses.example: The partners agreed to incorporate the new investor into the firm's ownership group.

senses.definition: To form into a legal company.
senses.example: The company was incorporated in 1980.

senses.definition: To include (another clause or guarantee of the US constitution) as a part (of the Fourteenth Amendment, such that the clause binds not only the federal government but also state governments).
senses.example: Over time, courts have incorporated most of the Bill of Rights into the Fourteenth Amendment.

senses.definition: To form into a body; to combine, as different ingredients, into one consistent mass.
senses.example: Gently incorporate the flour into the butter until the dough holds together.

senses.definition: To unite with a material body; to give a material form to; to embody.
senses.example: The sculptor's bronze figures incorporate the sorrow of her village's history.

senses.definition: Not consisting of matter; not having a material body; incorporeal; spiritual.
senses.example: Many medieval theologians argued that the soul is incorporate and cannot decay.

senses.definition: Not incorporated; not existing as a corporation.
senses.example: an incorporate banking association

core.definition: To include something as a part of a larger whole, or to combine ideas, ingredients, or features into one thing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of 'KOR', not the last. Keep the r clear in American speech, and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa. The verb ends with a clear 'rayt', while the noun is 'in-kor-puh-RAY-shun' with the stress shifting.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes integration and can be positive when describing useful combination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this verb in business, cooking, writing, and technology: 'We need to incorporate customer feedback into the design.' In cooking it means mixing an ingredient in. In legal or business contexts, 'incorporate' also means forming a corporation, a separate meaning. Casually, people often say 'include' or 'add' instead.

distinctions.note: Include is the everyday word for listing something among others; incorporate suggests blending the item fully into the whole.
Integrate implies making separate parts work together as a system; incorporate more often means taking something in as a component.

examples.everyday: Let's incorporate some fresh basil into the sauce before we serve it.
examples.professional: Can you incorporate the reviewers' comments into the draft before Friday's meeting?
examples.analytical: Aquinas incorporates Aristotle's categories into the structure of Christian moral theology without surrendering revelation.

nuance.analogy: Like adding flour to a batter: once mixed in, it can no longer be picked out as separate.
nuance.etymology: From Latin incorporare 'to embody, unite in one body', from in- + corpus 'body'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable; the verb stress is on the first syllable, in-KOR-puh-rayt.
Using 'incorporate to' instead of 'incorporate into' when describing combination.

incorporate.etymology: From Middle English, from Late Latin *incorporātus*, perfect passive participle of *incorporō* (“to embody, to incorporate”), from *in-* (“in”) + *corpus* (“body”).

senses.definition: (of a quantity, etc.) To become larger or greater, to greaten.
senses.example: His rage only increased when I told him of the lost money.

senses.definition: To make (a quantity, etc.) larger.
To multiply by the production of young; to be fertile, fruitful, or prolific.
To become more nearly full; to show more of the surface; to wax.
senses.example: The Moon increases.

senses.definition: An amount by which a quantity is increased.
senses.example: An increase of about 30% in hits on the website.

senses.definition: For a quantity, the act or process of becoming larger.
Offspring, progeny.
The creation of one or more new stitches; see Increase (knitting).

core.definition: To become larger or greater in amount, number, or degree; or to make something larger or greater.

pronunciation.tip: The verb stresses the second syllable, KREES, while the noun stresses the first syllable, IN-krees. Keep the first syllable short ('in', not 'een') and make the ending a clear, voiceless 's'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe good growth, such as income, or bad growth, such as prices or costs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'increase' in everyday news, business, and personal finance, as in 'Rent is going to increase next year.' In casual talk people often say 'go up,' which sounds more relaxed. You can say 'increase by 10 percent' or 'increase to 500 dollars,' and both are natural.

distinctions.note: Grow is more general and often used for living things or gradual change; increase emphasizes a measurable change in amount.
Rise is usually intransitive and often vertical, as in 'prices rose,' while increase can take an object, as in 'increase prices.'
Raise is transitive and often means to lift or raise a number or amount, as in 'raise the budget'; increase is broader and more formal.

examples.everyday: My landlord said the rent is going to increase next year, so we're looking at cheaper places.
examples.professional: Latency should decrease once we increase the cache size, so let's test it on staging first.
examples.analytical: The argument holds that as moral obligations increase in number, a finite agent must rank them, since no one can meet every duty at once.

nuance.analogy: Like a tide coming in: each wave adds a little more water until the level is clearly higher.
nuance.etymology: From Old French encreistre, from Latin increscere (to grow in), from in- and crescere (to grow).
common_mistakes: Using 'of' after the noun, as in 'an increase of price,' instead of the natural 'an increase in price.'
Saying 'increase up,' which is redundant; say 'increase' or 'go up.'
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 1:28 uses the Hebrew verbs parah (be fruitful) and rabah (multiply) for the blessing of growth, and in John 3:30 John the Baptist says that Christ must increase, using the Greek auxanō (to grow). Luke 2:52 describes Jesus increasing in wisdom and stature, using the Greek prokoptō (to advance).

increase.etymology: From Middle English *encresen*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *encreistre*, from Latin *increscō* (“to increase”), from *in* (“in, on”) + *crescō* (“grow”).

senses.definition: (obsolete) An investigator.
senses.label: obsolete

core.definition: An obsolete word for an investigator or inquirer, someone who searches for facts or the truth.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, IN. The second syllable is reduced to 'duh', and the final syllable is an American r-colored 'ur', as in 'water' with the r sound. Say IN-duh-gay-tur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical term for a seeker of facts with no negative or positive coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans do not use indagator in everyday or professional speech. It appears in older dictionaries, historical writing, or literary texts about detective work. Use investigator or inquirer in modern English.

distinctions.note: Investigator is the common modern term for someone who looks into a crime, a fact, or a question, while indagator is obsolete.
Inquirer is still used for someone who asks questions, while indagator is a historical term for someone who searches out facts.

examples.professional: The seventeenth-century dictionary lists indagator as an obsolete term for an investigator.
examples.analytical: Indagator, an archaic term for an inquirer, reflects an older view of inquiry as patient tracking of the truth.

nuance.analogy: An indagator is like a bloodhound of the old days: someone who follows the trail until the facts are found.
nuance.etymology: From Latin indagator, 'tracker, investigator', from indagare, 'to track down'.
common_mistakes: Using indagator in a modern report. Investigator is the correct everyday term.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable. Keep the second vowel reduced, not a full 'gay'.

senses.definition: In an equation, any variable whose value is not dependent on any other in the equation.
senses.example: In the equation z = x + y, x and y are the independent variables.

senses.definition: The variable that is changed or manipulated in a series of experiments.

core.definition: In an experiment, the variable the researcher changes or controls, whose effect on another variable is measured.

pronunciation.tip: The phrase has two main stresses: PEN in 'independent' and VAIR in 'variable.' Keep the final syllables reduced, so 'variable' sounds like 'VAIR-ee-uh-bul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in science, statistics and social research papers. In a lab or classroom it is the factor you manipulate. In ordinary talk people rarely use it, but a natural phrase is 'the independent variable is the dosage.' Its counterpart is the dependent variable.

distinctions.note: The independent variable is changed by the researcher, while the dependent variable is the outcome that is measured.
A control variable is held constant, while an independent variable is deliberately varied.

examples.everyday: My daughter's science fair project asked which variable she changed, and her teacher said the independent variable was the amount of water.
examples.professional: In our A/B test, the independent variable is the button color, and the dependent variable is the click-through rate.
examples.analytical: The independent variable must be manipulated in a way that isolates its causal effect on the outcome, not merely its correlation.

nuance.analogy: Like the dial you turn on a stove: you choose the setting, and the temperature of the pot is what you watch change.
nuance.etymology: 'Independent' from Latin independere, 'not to depend.' 'Variable' from Latin variabilis, 'changeable.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the independent variable with the dependent variable.
Stressing the wrong syllable in 'variable' and saying VAR-ee-uh-bul with a long a.

senses.definition: The quality of being indomitable.
The quality of being undefeated, resolute, and tenacious.

core.definition: The quality of refusing to be defeated, discouraged, or controlled, and keeping one's determination under pressure.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BIL, the fourth syllable, while the first syllable has a weaker secondary stress. The -ity ending is reduced to 'uh-tee', and the a in 'dah' is the cot vowel used in most of the US.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises strength, courage, and refusal to give up, and it often describes people in difficult situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun in speeches, essays, obituaries, and writing about history or sports. It is more common in written and formal speech than in casual talk.
