examples.analytical: Critics called the Tractarians ritualists, though many of them regarded liturgical form as the outward expression of doctrine rather than mere habit.

nuance.analogy: A ritualist is like a chef who will not cook a dish without measuring every ingredient in the exact order the recipe prescribes.
nuance.etymology: From ritual, from Latin ritualis, from ritus meaning religious custom, plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Using ritualist as an adjective; say ritualistic, as in a ritualistic dance, not a ritualist dance.
Stressing the last syllable or saying the middle as ri-TOO-al; stress belongs on the first syllable.

senses.definition: A cylindrical mechanical fastener which is supplied with a factory head at one end and is used to attach multiple parts together by passing its bucktail through a hole and upsetting its end to form a field head.
senses.example: The engineer checked each rivet along the steel seam for signs of corrosion.

senses.definition: Any fixed point or certain basis.
senses.example: Her daily prayers became the rivet around which her whole life turned through every hardship.

senses.definition: To attach or fasten parts by using rivets.
senses.example: The workers riveted the aluminum panels to the frame before the paint had dried.

senses.definition: To install rivets (see Usage notes).
senses.example: The crew riveted the hull plates using pneumatic hammers all through the long night shift.

senses.definition: To command the attention of.
senses.example: The stunning soprano riveted the audience from the first note to the final bow.

senses.definition: To make firm or immovable.
senses.example: Terror riveted him to the spot.

core.definition: A short metal pin with a head at one end, hammered at the other to hold metal pieces together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the final syllable a weak, quick schwa, not a full et sound. The t is often softened to a flap between vowels in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, technical word in engineering and manufacturing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rivet as a noun for a metal fastener, most often in construction, aircraft, and manufacturing. As a verb, it is common in the phrase 'riveted by' to mean fascinated, as in 'We were riveted by the story.' Casual speakers use it this way all the time.

distinctions.note: A screw is turned into place and can be removed, while a rivet is permanent and is set by deforming one end.
A bolt usually goes with a nut and can be taken apart, while a rivet is generally a permanent fastener.

examples.everyday: My kid is riveted by the documentary about bridge construction, especially the part about the old steel rivets.
examples.professional: The maintenance crew replaced several corroded rivets on the wing panel before the inspection.
examples.analytical: The rivet is a useful image in engineering texts because it shows how permanent joints depend on careful deformation.

nuance.analogy: A rivet is like a permanent staple for metal: once it is set, the parts stay together.
nuance.etymology: From Old French rivet, from river, to clinch or fasten the end of a nail or pin.
common_mistakes: Using rivet as a verb to mean screwing something in.
Saying the word with a long final ay or ett sound instead of a reduced schwa.

rivet.etymology: From Old French *rivet* (13th century), from the verb Old French *river* (“to fetter [a person]”) (12th century), from Old French *rive* (“rim, edge”) (ca.

senses.definition: The construction or maintenance done to roads.
senses.example: The traffic jam was caused by roadwork being done during rush hour.

senses.definition: Exercise such as running and jogging done on the roads.
senses.example: The athlete needed to get home early to do his roadwork before it got too dark to be safe.

senses.definition: The taking of a band on the road to perform music in different locations.
senses.example: The band spent the spring on road work, playing clubs in twelve states.

core.definition: Construction or repair work being done on a road, often causing delays or lane closures for drivers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WORK, with the r in both words pronounced clearly. The vowel in WORK is the American stressed er sound, so do not say 'walk' or 'wok'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, since it usually means delays and inconvenience for drivers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say road work for construction crews fixing a road, and they often see it on signs such as 'Road Work Ahead.' In a conversation you might say 'Sorry I'm late, there was road work on the highway.' Note that in the sense of running or jogging, the phrase is rare; Americans would say 'running' or 'training.'

distinctions.note: Construction is a broader term for building projects, while road work is specifically about roads being built, repaired or maintained.
A detour is the alternate route you take because of road work or another closure, not the work itself.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, there was road work on Main Street and traffic was crawling.
examples.professional: The city's road work schedule will affect two intersections downtown, so please plan for extra travel time next month.
examples.analytical: Road work reveals how public infrastructure is often invisible until it disrupts daily routines and forces drivers to notice the systems they rely on.

nuance.analogy: Road work is like a kitchen remodel in a busy house: everyone notices it only when it slows down their daily routine.
nuance.etymology: Road comes from Old English rād, meaning riding or a journey; work comes from Old English weorc.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing road work as 'row' in the sense of a road, when road rhymes with 'code' in American English.
Writing roadwork as one word in formal writing, when road work is the standard two-word form in most sources.

conversation.text: There's road work on Elm Street, so take Oak instead.
Road work season in Michigan seems to last all summer.
The sign said "Road Work Ahead," so I slowed down.

senses.definition: Very hot.
senses.example: The day started out cool, but by noon it was roasting.

senses.definition: The act by which something is roasted.
senses.example: The roasting of the coffee beans filled the kitchen with a rich, nutty aroma.

senses.definition: A strong rebuke or reprimand (usually from the recipient's point of view).
senses.example: My boss gave me a roasting for last month's sales figures.

senses.definition: The act of attempting to humiliating someone or being humiliated in such a way that it appears comedic, especially publicly.
senses.example: The group chat turned into a roasting session, with everyone teasing Mark about his haircut.

core.definition: Extremely hot, as in weather or a room that is uncomfortably warm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the 'st' cluster clean, with no flap. The -ing ending is a short /ɪŋ/, not a long 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous, depending on context; it describes uncomfortable heat but can be a playful complaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'It's roasting out here' or 'It's roasting in this car' in casual conversation to complain about heat, usually in summer. The word is informal and a bit exaggerated, so it is less suitable for formal writing. As a noun, 'roasting' can also mean a strong scolding or a comic public humiliation, which is a separate sense.

distinctions.note: Sweltering describes oppressive, humid heat and sounds more formal or literary; roasting is more casual and focuses on dry, intense warmth.
Boiling is an informal word for hot weather in American speech, but it is less intense than roasting.

examples.everyday: It's roasting out there, so let's grab an iced coffee before we walk to the park.
examples.professional: The server room is roasting, so we need to check the cooling system before the next deployment.
examples.analytical: The poem's imagery of a roasting desert noon makes the landscape feel hostile and almost alive.

nuance.analogy: Roasting weather is like standing too close to an open oven: the heat surrounds you and makes every breath feel heavy.
nuance.etymology: From the verb roast, with the -ing ending used adjectivally.
common_mistakes: Using 'roasting' in very formal writing, where 'extremely hot' or 'oppressively warm' is more appropriate.
Pronouncing the final -ing as 'eeng' instead of a short 'ing' sound.

senses.definition: A projectile.
senses.example: The rebels fired a crude rocket over the border fence at dawn.

senses.definition: A cylindrical projectile that can be fired to a great height through combustion, a type of firework of this form, typically exploding with light and color; a skyrocket.
senses.example: The crowd cheered as a red rocket burst over the lake.

senses.definition: A blunt lance head used in jousting.
senses.example: Before the tournament, the squire swapped the sharp lance for a blunt rocket.

senses.definition: A long vehicle or craft propelled by a rocket engine; a missile or rocket-propelled spacecraft.
An engine operating similarly to the pyrotechnic, generating thrust by the expulsion of hot gases; a rocket engine.
senses.example: The rocket's engine roared as the shuttle lifted off the launch pad.

senses.definition: Figurative uses.
Something that travels high in the air or with great speed; especially, a hard shot.
senses.example: His rocket from the blue line flew past the goalie into the top corner.

senses.definition: An ace (the playing card).
senses.example: He slammed down the rocket and claimed the final trick of the hand.

senses.definition: A leaf vegetable of species Eruca sativa or Eruca vesicaria.
senses.example: We tossed arugula, which some grocers call rocket, into the spring salad.

senses.definition: Any plant of the genus Eruca.
senses.example: The garden center sold rocket seeds alongside the basil and mint.

senses.definition: Rocket larkspur (Consolida regalis, syn. Delphinium consolida).
senses.example: The cottage garden bloomed with rocket larkspur every early summer.

senses.definition: To accelerate swiftly and powerfully.
senses.example: Her startup's revenue rocketed after the product launch exceeded expectations.

senses.definition: To fly vertically.
senses.example: The jet rocketed straight up after takeoff, pressing us into our seats.

senses.definition: To rise or soar rapidly.
senses.example: Gas prices rocketed in the weeks after the hurricane hit the coast.

senses.definition: To experience sudden fame, popularity, or success.
senses.example: After spending years in obscurity, the band finally rocketed last week.

senses.definition: To carry something in a rocket.
senses.example: The mission rockets fresh supplies to the space station every quarter.

senses.definition: To attack something with rockets.
senses.example: Insurgents rocketed the military base just after midnight, waking everyone nearby.

core.definition: A vehicle or missile propelled by burning fuel, used to launch spacecraft, carry weapons, or as a firework.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAH. The second syllable is a weak 'kit' with a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'RAH-kit,' not 'rock-ET.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical and news contexts; positive when describing fast success, as in 'a rocket ship' rise in sales.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rocket for spacecraft launches, military weapons, and fireworks, and in news reports about missile attacks. In everyday speech, it is common to talk about a rocket launch or a model rocket. The idiom 'It's not rocket science' is very common in workplace talk meaning the task is not very hard.

distinctions.note: A missile is usually guided and carries a warhead; a rocket may be unguided and is defined by its propulsion.
A spacecraft is what travels in space, while a rocket is the vehicle that lifts it there.

examples.everyday: The kids watched a model rocket launch from the backyard last Saturday.
examples.professional: The launch team checked the rocket's fuel system before the countdown started.
examples.analytical: Rocketry turns Newton's third law into practical engineering, since every thrust depends on expelling mass backward.

nuance.analogy: A rocket works like a balloon releasing air: the escaping gas pushes the balloon forward.
nuance.etymology: From Italian rochetta, a diminutive of rocca, meaning distaff, the spindle used in spinning.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in rock-ET.
Confusing rocket with racket, which has a different meaning and sound.

rocket.etymology: From Italian *rocchetta*, from Old Italian *rocchetto* (“rocket”), diminutive of *rocca* (“a distaff”), from *rocko* (“spinning wheel”), from **rokkō*, from Proto-Germanic **rukkô* (“a distaff, a staff with flax fibres tied loosely to it, used in spinning…

senses.definition: One who, or that which, roots; one that tears up by the roots.
A type of heavy machinery similar to a plow for breaking up soil, concrete, asphalt, etc.
A blade for producing a narrow groove in a piece of wood.
A device for boring a pathway through a blocked drain or sewer.
One who roots or rummages through something.
A type of malware that obtains and runs using privileged access, bypassing normal security systems.
One who holds a primary or founding position in an enterprise.
A plant, viewed in terms of how it establishes its roots.
One who roots for, or applauds, something.

core.definition: A person who enthusiastically supports a sports team or player; a fan who cheers loudly for one side.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is an unstressed r-colored vowel, not a separate 'ter' syllable. Keep the vowel in 'roo' long and do not confuse it with 'router' (/ˈɹaʊtɚ/), the networking device.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes loyal, enthusiastic support. It is friendly and can be used playfully about yourself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'rooter' mostly in sports talk, as in 'a big Cubs rooter' or 'home-team rooters', and it sounds casual and friendly. Most people say 'fan' in general, and 'rooter' sounds a bit old-fashioned or folksy in some settings. Outside sports, 'rooter' can also mean a machine or tool that tears up roots or soil, and a plumber's root-cutting tool is also called a rooter.

distinctions.note: 'Fan' is the general and most common word; 'rooter' stresses vocal, active cheering at a game.
'Supporter' is broader and more formal, and can refer to any cause or politician, while 'rooter' is mostly about sports.

collocations: a big rooter for the Cubs

examples.everyday: My dad is a huge rooter for the Packers, so he yells at the TV every Sunday.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants to reach local rooters who buy season tickets to the minor league team.
examples.analytical: Being a rooter for one side makes a fan notice the referee's mistakes against that side and overlook the same mistakes for the other.

nuance.analogy: A rooter is like a cheerleader who sits in the stands, sending energy from the crowd to the players.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'root' in its nineteenth-century American sense 'to cheer on'; the exact origin of that sense is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'rooter' with 'router', the networking device, which is pronounced differently.
Saying 'rooter' without the verb form: people say 'root for the team', not 'rooter the team'.

senses.definition: Redness or blushing.
Ruddle or red ochre.
To become red; redden.
senses.example: Her cheeks rud at the compliment, and she looked away shyly.

core.definition: Redness or a blush; in older English, the color red or red ochre.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with a short 'uh' vowel, like 'bud' or 'mud'. The r is a full American r at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is rare and old-fashioned, so it sounds antique rather than emotional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use rud today. You may see it in older dictionaries, poetry, or historical texts. In everyday talk, say 'redness' or 'a blush' instead.

distinctions.note: Ruddy is a common adjective for a reddish face; rud is an archaic noun for the redness itself.
A blush is a common, everyday word for reddening of the face from embarrassment; rud is archaic.

examples.everyday: Her rud gave away her embarrassment before she could say a word.
examples.professional: The historical text refers to a rud pigment used for the manuscript borders.
examples.analytical: The archaic term rud preserves an older sense of redness that the modern word 'redness' has largely lost.

nuance.analogy: Like a faded old word preserved in an antique book, still readable but no longer in daily use.
nuance.etymology: From Old English rudu, 'redness,' related to Old English read, 'red.'
common_mistakes: Using rud in modern conversation, where it will sound odd.
Confusing it with 'rude' or 'rod'.

senses.definition: A fold, crease or wrinkle.

core.definition: A fold, crease or wrinkle, especially a small ridge in skin or in the lining of an organ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long 'oo.' The second syllable is a weak 'uh,' and the 'g' is a hard 'g,' as in 'go.' In technical plural 'rugae,' say 'ROO-jee' or 'ROO-gye.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise descriptive term without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet 'ruga' in anatomy, dentistry, dermatology or forensic science. In everyday talk they say 'wrinkle,' 'crease' or 'fold.' In technical writing, the plural 'rugae' is standard, and dentists often use it when discussing the ridges on the roof of the mouth.

distinctions.note: 'Wrinkle' is the everyday word for lines in skin or fabric, while 'ruga' is a technical term for a fold or ridge in anatomy or surfaces.
A crease is often a sharp, deliberate line, such as in trousers, while a ruga is a natural, usually small ridge.
'Fold' is general and common, while 'ruga' specifically names a small, patterned ridge or wrinkle in tissue.

examples.everyday: At the dentist, she pointed to the ridges on the roof of my mouth and called them rugae.
examples.professional: The forensic report notes that the palatal rugae pattern matched the dental records.
examples.analytical: The gastric rugae flatten when the stomach fills, which is why the inner surface looks smooth after a large meal.

nuance.analogy: A ruga is like the ridges on a corduroy fabric: small, regular folds that make a surface textured and recognizable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'ruga,' meaning wrinkle or fold.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'ruga' with 'rug,' the floor covering.
Using 'rugas' as the plural in technical writing; the standard plural is 'rugae.'
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'roo-GAH.'

senses.definition: To be late; to fail to be on time.
senses.example: If the bus runs late again, I'll miss my first class and the quiz.

core.definition: To be later than the planned or expected time for something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LATE, with run lighter. The r in run is clear in American speech, and late has a long a sound like 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common courtesy situation, though it can sound slightly negative if you cause repeated delays.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm running late or running ten minutes late to tell someone they should expect you soon, and it is polite to text a colleague or friend when this happens. Running late suggests you are still on your way, while be late is the plain fact. A natural reply is 'No worries, we're just starting.'

distinctions.note: Be late is the neutral fact, while run late implies you are still on the way and trying to arrive soon.
Behind schedule is more formal and usually describes projects or plans rather than personal arrivals.

collocations: let them know you're running late

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm running about ten minutes late, so start the coffee without me.
examples.professional: The vendor demo is running late, so let's push the review to 3:30 and send the slides in advance.
examples.analytical: A person who habitually runs late often treats punctuality as a matter of respect for others' time, not merely a question of the clock.

nuance.analogy: Like a train leaving the station a few minutes behind, you are still moving, just not on the timetable.
nuance.etymology: Run from Old English rinnan; late from Old English læt, meaning slow.
common_mistakes: Confusing late with lately, which means recently, as in 'I'm running lately'
Saying 'I run late' for a specific occasion instead of 'I'm running late'

senses.definition: The property of being sapient, the property of possessing or being able to possess wisdom.
senses.example: Her sermon praised the sapience of ancient rabbis who valued patient study over quick answers.

core.definition: Wisdom; the capacity for thoughtful judgment and sound understanding, especially the ability to reason well about life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAY, and the ending -ence is reduced to 'uns', not 'ens'. The vowel in 'pee' is long and clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises wisdom and the capacity for judgment, though it is rare and can sound pretentious in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Sapience is an uncommon, mostly literary or academic word for wisdom, especially the capacity for thoughtful judgment. Americans would more often say wisdom or good judgment in everyday speech. It appears in philosophy, science fiction and discussions of artificial intelligence, but it rarely fits casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Wisdom is the everyday word, while sapience is a more formal or academic term for the capacity to reason and judge well.
Intelligence is the ability to learn and solve problems, while sapience emphasizes sound judgment rather than mere cleverness.
Sentience is the capacity to feel and experience, while sapience is the capacity for wisdom; the two are often confused in discussions of AI or animal minds.

examples.everyday: My grandmother had a quiet sapience that made people come to her for advice.
examples.professional: When we hire for the ethics board, we look for sapience and judgment, not just technical skill.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers treated sapience as a gift of God that distinguishes humans from the beasts, and that gift carries moral responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Sapience is the difference between knowing many facts and knowing which facts matter for a good decision.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sapientia 'wisdom,' from sapiens 'wise,' from sapere 'to be wise, to taste.'
common_mistakes: Confusing sapience, meaning wisdom, with sentience, meaning the capacity to feel.
Saying SAY-pee-ence with a full final syllable; the ending is reduced.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word hokhmah (wisdom, skill in living) is rendered in the Latin Vulgate as sapientia, and the Greek Septuagint uses sophia. The Book of Proverbs presents wisdom as beginning with reverence for the LORD, a theme also expressed in Job 28:28. Proverbs 1:7 links reverence for the LORD with the beginning of knowledge, and Proverbs 9:10 says the same of wisdom. These passages show that biblical sapience is grounded in right relationship with God, not in mere cleverness.

sapience.etymology: From Middle English *sapience*, from Old French *sapience*, from Latin *sapientia*.

senses.definition: To prevent harm or difficulty.
senses.example: She was saved from drowning by a passer-by.

senses.definition: To help (somebody) to survive, or rescue (somebody or something) from harm.
senses.example: She was saved from drowning by a passer-by.

senses.definition: To keep (something) safe; to safeguard.
senses.example: We bought a fireproof safe to save our family's important documents from fire.

senses.definition: To spare (somebody) (from effort, or from something undesirable).
senses.example: Hiring a dishwasher will save you from scrubbing pots every night after dinner.

senses.definition: To redeem, protect, rescue, or keep (someone) from eternal damnation.
senses.example: Jesus Christ came to save sinners.

senses.definition: To put aside; to avoid.
senses.example: Let's save the packaging in case we need to send the product back.

senses.definition: To store for future use.
senses.example: Let's save the packaging in case we need to send the product back.

senses.definition: To conserve or prevent the wasting of.
senses.example: Save electricity by turning off the lights when you leave the room.

senses.definition: To obviate or make unnecessary.
senses.example: Ordering groceries online will save us a trip to the store this week.

senses.definition: To write (a file) to disk or other storage medium.
senses.example: Where did I save that document? I can't find it on the desktop.

senses.definition: To economize or avoid waste, often with on.
senses.example: We try to save on utilities by turning off lights and heating unused rooms.

senses.definition: To accumulate (money or other valuables or resources), often with up and/or for.
senses.example: (transitive) I'm trying to save enough money for a new car.

senses.definition: To refrain from romantic or sexual relationships until one is married or is with a suitable partner.
senses.example: She told me she's saving herself for marriage.

senses.definition: To repress or avoid saying (something).
senses.example: Save your excuses and lies.

senses.definition: To catch or deflect (a shot at goal).
senses.example: The goalie made a diving stop to save the shot near the post.

senses.definition: To preserve, as a relief pitcher, (a win of another pitcher's on one's team) by defending the lead held when the other pitcher left the game.
senses.example: He came in from the bullpen to save the game after the starter tired in the seventh.

senses.definition: An instance of preventing (further) harm or difficulty.
senses.example: The goaltender made a great save.

senses.definition: In various sports, a block that prevents an opponent from scoring.
senses.example: The goaltender made a great save.

senses.definition: A point in a professional wrestling match when one or more wrestlers run to the ring to aid a fellow wrestler who is being beaten.
senses.example: The giant wrestler continued to beat down his smaller opponent, until several wrestlers ran in for the save.

senses.definition: An action that brings one back out of an awkward situation.
senses.example: Nice save.

senses.definition: The act, process, or result of saving data to a storage medium.
senses.example: If you're hit by a power cut, you'll lose all of your changes since your last save.

senses.definition: A saving throw.
senses.example: She rolled a natural twenty and made her Wisdom save easily.

senses.definition: A successful attempt by a relief pitcher to preserve the win of another pitcher on one's team.
senses.example: Jones retired seven to earn the save.

senses.definition: Except; with the exception of.
senses.example: Everyone in the office showed up for the meeting save Brian, who was sick.

senses.definition: Unless; except.
senses.example: We would have left early, save that the traffic was already terrible.

core.definition: To rescue someone or something from harm, danger or loss, or to keep it from being wasted.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with wave and has a single syllable. The final v is voiced, so do not add a vowel and say 'sayv-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests protection, rescue or wise use of resources, and it is one of the most common words in daily English.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use save constantly, both for rescue (save a life, save a drowning child) and for money, time and energy (save money, save time). In sports, a save is a goalkeeper or goalie stopping a shot. A common casual reply to a favor is 'You saved my life' or 'Thanks, you're a lifesaver.'

distinctions.note: Rescue implies pulling someone out of immediate danger, while save can also mean preventing a future loss or conserving something.
Keep means holding onto something; save adds the idea of protecting it from loss, harm or waste.
Store means putting something away for later use, while save often implies preventing harm or waste as well.

examples.everyday: Thanks for grabbing that bag before it fell, you saved me a trip back to the car.
examples.professional: If we automate the nightly data load, we can save the analytics team about ten hours a week.
examples.analytical: The argument turns on whether to save someone means to remove a danger or to transform the person who is in danger.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard who pulls a swimmer out before the current takes over, save means stepping in before the loss becomes permanent.
nuance.etymology: From Old French sauver, from Latin salvare, to make safe, from salvus, safe or whole.
common_mistakes: Saying 'save someone to drown' instead of 'save someone from drowning'; the preposition from is needed.
Saying 'save my time' instead of 'save me time' or 'save time'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek verb is soz\u014d (s\u014dz\u014d), meaning to save, rescue, heal or make whole. Matthew 1:21 says the child will save his people from their sins. Luke 19:10 says the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Ephesians 2:8 says that people are saved by grace through faith, not by their own works.

save.etymology: From Middle English *saven*, *sauven*, a borrowing from Old French *sauver*, from Late Latin *salvo* (“to save”).

senses.definition: A person who commits fraud by making dishonest scams and business deals: swindler, cheat, grifter.
senses.example: The scammer posed as a bank officer and emptied the elderly man's savings account.

core.definition: A person who cheats others out of money or property through deception, often by phone, email, or online.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light, r-colored 'er' with no extra vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the second syllable or pronounce the 'a' as in 'father'; the 'a' should be short, as in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. The word always describes someone dishonest who takes advantage of others, and it is used in news reports and everyday warnings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scammer for people who run fraudulent schemes, such as fake prize notices, phone calls pretending to be from the IRS, or online romance fraud. It is informal but very common in conversation and the news. For a more formal or legal context, Americans may say fraudster or con artist instead.

distinctions.note: Fraudster is more formal and often used in legal or financial reporting, while scammer is everyday language for anyone running a scheme.
Con artist emphasizes the skill and charm of the deception, while scammer focuses more simply on the dishonest act.

collocations: scammer posing as a bank employee

examples.everyday: My mom almost sent money to a scammer who said he was her grandson.
examples.professional: Our security team flagged a scammer who was impersonating one of our vendors in invoice emails.
examples.analytical: Calling the fraudster a scammer reduces a systemic problem to a matter of individual bad character.

nuance.analogy: A scammer is like a wolf in sheep's clothing, looking friendly until it is too late.
nuance.etymology: Agent noun from scam; the origin of scam itself is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (scam-ER) instead of the first
Pronouncing the 'a' as in 'father' rather than the short 'a' in 'cat'

senses.definition: To collect and remove refuse, or to search through refuse, carrion, or abandoned items for useful material.
senses.example: We scavenged a couple of old beer cans for our art project.

senses.definition: To remove unwanted material from something, especially to purify molten metal by removing impurities.
To expel the exhaust gases from the cylinder of an internal combustion engine, and draw in air for the next cycle.
To feed on carrion or refuse.

core.definition: To search through discarded things to find something useful that others have left behind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, so the word has only two full syllables, and the final j sound is the same as in 'judge.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it can suggest desperation or scrounging, or simply resourcefulness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scavenge for finding parts, food, or materials in unlikely places, such as a garage full of old things or a neighborhood curb on trash day. It can be a little informal and implies searching rather than buying. In technical talk, it also describes engines and metals.

distinctions.note: Forage usually means searching for food in nature, while scavenge is about finding useful items among discarded things.
Search is general; scavenge specifically suggests digging through leftovers or junk to find something usable.

examples.everyday: We scavenged a few good chairs from the curb after the neighbors moved out.
examples.professional: The team scavenged spare servers from the decommissioned lab to keep the pilot running.
examples.analytical: Scavenging is a survival strategy that depends on what the environment discards.

nuance.analogy: Scavenging is like a bird picking through crumbs after a picnic to find something still worth eating.
nuance.etymology: From scavenger, from Middle English scavager, an official who collected tolls, from scavage, a customs duty.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as a full vowel, 'SKAV-en-j,' instead of the reduced schwa.
Using scavenge only for animals, when Americans also use it for people finding useful items.

senses.definition: Having a pleasant aroma.
Having a smell of any kind.
senses.example: a plant with skunk-scented leaves

senses.definition: Having perfume added.
senses.example: a scented soap

core.definition: Having a pleasant smell, often because perfume, oil or soap has been added to it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a short, reduced vowel, so it sounds like SEN-tid, not SEN-tayd. The -ed after a t is pronounced id.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, describing a pleasant added smell. It is neutral when describing a product plainly, and can be negative in phrases like heavily scented, which suggests too much perfume.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scented mostly for products: scented candles, scented lotion, unscented detergent. Calling a person scented is unusual and can suggest they wear too much perfume. For a naturally pleasant smell in conversation, people more often say fragrant or smells nice.

distinctions.note: Fragrant suggests a pleasant, often natural or sweet smell and sounds more literary; scented often means a smell that has been added to a product.
Perfumed means treated with perfume and sounds more deliberate; scented is the everyday word for any product with an added smell.

examples.everyday: I bought those lavender-scented candles because they make the living room smell like a spa.
examples.professional: The new hand soap is lightly scented, so it works well for the front desk and the break room.
examples.analytical: Scented products shape the sensory experience of a room, so the choice of fragrance is never purely a matter of personal taste.

nuance.analogy: A scented object is like a plain room that someone has painted: its natural state has been changed by an added layer of smell.
nuance.etymology: From scent plus the suffix -ed; scent comes from Old French sentir, from Latin sentire, meaning to feel or perceive.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two full syllables, SEN-ti-ded, instead of SEN-tid.
Using scented for a person's natural body odor; say has a smell or smells instead.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being scentless.

core.definition: The state of having no smell, or of lacking the scent expected from something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final two syllables are reduced to a soft us-nus sound. Keep the first syllable strong and let the rest be quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is rarely used in everyday speech and can sound stiff.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use scentlessness in ordinary conversation. It appears in technical or literary descriptions, such as product testing or nature writing. In everyday speech, people say the lack of smell or that something has no smell.

distinctions.note: Odorlessness is the more technical noun used in chemistry and safety contexts; scentlessness is more descriptive and often applies to flowers or products.

examples.professional: The test measures the scentlessness of the new packaging material before it goes into production.
examples.analytical: The scentlessness of the flower is a feature of its evolutionary strategy, since it may rely on color rather than smell to attract pollinators.

nuance.analogy: Scentlessness is like silence in a room that should be full of music: the absence is noticed because a sense expected something.
nuance.etymology: From scentless plus the suffix -ness, forming a noun of state.
common_mistakes: Using scentlessness in casual speech where no smell is clearer.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sent-less-NESS.

senses.definition: A bag of cannabis worth £20.
senses.example: Dealers in the park sold scores to students every weekend night.

senses.definition: Plural of score.
Third-person singular simple present indicative of score.

core.definition: Third-person singular of score: to earn points, goals or runs in a game, or to get a particular result on a test.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable. The final s is pronounced as a z sound, because it follows a voiced consonant, so it sounds like 'skorz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it reports an action or result, and can sound positive when someone scores well.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'She scores' or 'He scores' during sports, and 'scores well' or 'scores high' for tests and surveys. As the plural noun, 'scores' can mean many people or things, as in 'scores of fans,' which means dozens, not an exact count of twenty. The old meaning of score as twenty is rarely used today.

distinctions.note: Scores of means dozens, a large number, not an exact count of twenty.
Scored is the past tense; scores is for the present with he, she or it.

examples.everyday: She scores a goal in almost every game this season, which makes the coach happy.
examples.professional: The new vendor scores higher than the old one on every metric in our evaluation.
examples.analytical: Each candidate's argument scores well on logic but poorly on sources, which changes the overall judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermometer reading that rises or falls, showing where a performance stands.
nuance.etymology: From score, the third-person singular form of the verb.
common_mistakes: Using the present form after a past time word, as in 'She scores two goals yesterday'; say 'scored'.
Thinking scores of always means exactly twenty.

senses.definition: Thorough, careful, strict.

core.definition: Examining something very closely and thoroughly, often with a critical or suspicious eye.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKROO-, and reduce the final -ous to a quiet 'us'. The middle -ti- sounds like 'tuh', not 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it describes close, critical examination and can suggest intrusive or suspicious attention, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly in writing and formal speech about careful review, such as reports, audits or editorials. In everyday talk they would more often say 'careful' or 'close'. Calling someone scrutinous about their own work is a compliment, but being scrutinous about your personal life can sound like an accusation.

distinctions.note: Scrupulous means carefully attentive to moral right and wrong or exact standards; scrutinous means examining something closely for flaws or facts.
Meticulous stresses extreme attention to small details and precision; scrutinous stresses critical, searching examination.

examples.everyday: Our landlord is really scrutinous about the security deposit, so he checked every corner of the apartment.
examples.professional: The compliance team was scrutinous in reviewing the vendor contract before we signed it.
examples.analytical: A scrutinous reading of the text reveals assumptions that the author never states outright.

nuance.analogy: Like a jeweler examining a stone under a loupe, where nothing escapes the close look.
nuance.etymology: From Latin scrutari 'to search, examine'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'scrupulous' (morally careful), which is a different word.
Using it for a casual glance; it implies deliberate, critical examination.

senses.definition: In a secondary manner or degree.
senses.example: Primarily, this will cause deaths; secondarily, it will also cost a lot of money.

senses.definition: With lesser importance.
senses.example: Primarily, this will cause deaths; secondarily, it will also cost a lot of money.

core.definition: In a less important way; as an additional or secondary matter after the main one.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DAIR, and the final -ary is reduced to a weak 'uh'. Many non-native speakers stress the first syllable, which sounds unnatural to Americans.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is precise and formal, mostly used in writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing, reports, academic work and formal speech to show a second level of importance. In everyday conversation they say 'also' or 'on top of that'. It works well paired with 'primarily' to make a clear contrast.

distinctions.note: Secondly introduces the second point in a list, while secondarily describes a less important role or effect.
Additionally adds information neutrally, while secondarily signals that something ranks lower in importance.
Incidentally means by the way, a casual aside, not a formal ranking of importance.

examples.everyday: The den is mostly for watching TV, and secondarily it is our guest room.
examples.professional: This dashboard is built primarily for analysts and secondarily for executives who want a summary.
examples.analytical: The author reads the text primarily as doctrine and secondarily as a record of community practice.

nuance.analogy: Like a spare tire: useful and sometimes needed, but not the main way you drive.
nuance.etymology: From secondary, from Latin secundarius, of the second rank, from secundus, second; -ly makes it an adverb.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SEC-un-dair-uh-lee
Using it in casual speech where 'also' sounds more natural
Confusing it with 'secondly', which introduces a numbered point

senses.definition: A person who keeps records, takes notes and handles general clerical work.
senses.example: I have a personal secretary to help me organize my clients.

senses.definition: The head of a department of government.
senses.example: The Secretary of State announced the new trade agreement at a press conference.

senses.definition: A managerial or leading position in certain non-profit organizations, such as political parties, trade unions, international organizations.
senses.example: Ban Ki-Moon was a secretary general of the United Nations.

senses.definition: A type of desk, secretary desk; a secretaire.
senses.example: She kept her grandmother's mahogany secretary in the front hall for letters.

senses.definition: A secretary bird, a bird of the species Sagittarius serpentarius.
senses.example: On the African savanna, the secretary stalked snakes through the tall grass.

senses.definition: To serve as a secretary of.
senses.example: He secretaried for the dean of the seminary for six years before returning to teaching.

core.definition: A person whose job is to handle records, correspondence, scheduling, and other office support work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'SEK.' Pronounce every syllable clearly; many learners drop the middle 'r' or make the last syllable too long.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. For office work, it is a respectful job title, but in some modern offices people prefer 'administrative assistant.'
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, 'secretary' usually means an office worker who supports a manager. In government, 'Secretary' with a capital S is the head of a cabinet department, as in 'Secretary of State' or 'Secretary of Defense.' Americans rarely use 'secretary' as a verb, but the noun is common in offices and politics.

distinctions.note: 'Administrative assistant' is the most common modern US job title for office support, while 'secretary' is more traditional.
An assistant may help with many tasks, while a secretary traditionally focuses on records, scheduling, and correspondence.

examples.everyday: I called the doctor's office and the secretary said the appointment is Thursday.
examples.professional: Please send the meeting notes to the department secretary so she can file them.
examples.analytical: A secretary in the older sense was a confidential agent, and the modern office title preserves some of that trust.

nuance.analogy: Like a librarian for an office: she keeps the records organized and makes sure the right information reaches the right people.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin secretarius, 'confidant, private secretary,' from Latin secretum, 'secret.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'secretary' for a senior executive; in the US, an executive assistant or chief of staff is a different role.
Mispronouncing the middle 'ar' as 'ah' instead of a clear American 'air.'

secretary.etymology: From Medieval Latin *secrētārius* (“one entrusted with secrets”), from Latin *secrētus* (“private, secret”), past participle of *secerno* (“to separate, set apart”), from *se-* (“apart”) + *cerno* (“to separate”).

senses.definition: Without concern for one's own advantage; selfless or self-sacrificing.
senses.example: The nurse's self-denying work in the clinic earned her the respect of everyone.

core.definition: Giving up your own comfort, interests, or desires in order to help others or to live by a higher principle.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NYE, the second syllable, and the vowel is a diphthong that glides from ah to ee. Do not stress the first syllable, and do not pronounce the ending as a separate heavy syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive, because it praises generosity and sacrifice. It can sound overly pious or stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mostly in religious, literary, or formal speech, such as a sermon, a eulogy, or an essay: 'a self-denying parent.' In everyday conversation people usually say 'selfless' or 'unselfish.' Do not confuse the adjective with the noun self-denial, which is the act itself.

distinctions.note: Selfless is common and everyday, while self-denying suggests deliberately giving up things you want.
Altruistic is formal and focuses on benefiting others, while self-denying focuses on the personal cost of the sacrifice.
Generous describes the act of giving, while self-denying emphasizes the sacrifice that stands behind it.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was so self-denying that she never bought anything for herself, so we could have a nice Christmas.
examples.professional: The nonprofit's leaders took no salary for three years so the funds could go to the clinics, a self-denying choice the board still talks about.
examples.analytical: Some Christian ethicists read Jesus's call to self-denying discipleship as a call to reorder desire, not merely to suppress it.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who skips dessert all season so the body can perform at its best.
nuance.etymology: self + deny, from Latin negare, 'to say no'.
common_mistakes: Using 'self-denying' as a noun; the noun is self-denial
Assuming the word is negative; it is almost always admired
nuance.biblical_note: In the Gospels, the call to self-denial uses the Greek verb aparneomai, 'to deny, disown'. Jesus tells would-be followers to deny themselves and take up their cross in Mark 8:34, Matthew 16:24, and Luke 9:23 (RSV), where Luke adds the word 'daily'. In these passages self-denial is the first step of following Jesus, meaning giving up self-rule and trusting God, not merely giving up pleasures.

traditions.view: Catholic tradition links self-denial with penance, fasting, and almsgiving, especially during Lent, and sees it as cooperating with divine grace.
The Eastern Orthodox ascetic tradition treats self-denial as part of the ongoing struggle of fasting and prayer, aimed at purifying the heart and union with God.

Many Protestants, including Lutherans and the Reformed, treat self-denial as a fruit of faith rather than a means of earning God's favor, while practices like fasting vary widely among Anglicans, Baptists, and Pentecostals.

senses.definition: Send someone an invitation, often a calendar invitation for a meeting.
senses.example: Could you send an invite for Thursday's planning meeting to the whole design team?

core.definition: To send someone an invitation, especially a calendar invitation for a meeting or event.

pronunciation.tip: In 'send an invite', the noun 'invite' takes stress on IN, not on the verb's 'in-VITE'. The 'an' reduces to 'un' and links to 'send', so it sounds like 'sen-dun-IN-vite'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly; it sounds efficient and ordinary in workplace talk.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'invite' is the everyday word for a calendar event that others can accept. It is informal but normal in workplace chat and email. In a formal letter, write 'send an invitation' instead. Typical replies are 'Got it, thanks' or 'Sure, I'll accept.'

distinctions.note: Invitation is the formal noun for a written request; invite as a noun is more casual and common at work.
Microsoft Outlook calls it a meeting request, while other calendar apps say invite; the action is the same.

examples.everyday: I'll send you an invite to the birthday party, so just tell me which email to use.
examples.professional: I'll send an invite for Thursday's review, so please add your agenda items to the calendar entry.
examples.analytical: Calling the message a mere invite obscures its function as a binding request for attendance and contribution.

nuance.analogy: Like a name card at a dinner table: it saves a seat for you and asks you to respond.
nuance.etymology: Invite comes from Latin invitare, 'to invite, summon'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the verb form, saying 'send an in-VITE'; for the noun, the stress is IN-vite.
Saying 'send invitation to you' instead of 'send you an invitation'.

conversation.text: I'll send an invite for next week's review.
Can you send an invite to the whole team?
Let me know a good time, and I'll send an invite.

senses.definition: Chiefly in the plural: a condition or disease which follows chronologically after an earlier one, being either partly or wholly caused by it, or made possible by it.
That which follows; a consequence, an effect.
senses.example: The doctor monitored the patient closely for any sequela, especially infection, after the surgery.

senses.definition: (rare) People who adhere to the opinions or teachings of another; followers.
senses.example: Her sequela from the seminary filled the church pews every Sunday, quoting her teachings.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A condition, usually a disease or injury, that follows from an earlier one and is partly or wholly caused by it. Plural: sequelae.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWEE, the second syllable. In American speech the vowel is long 'ee', not the short 'eh' of British pronunciations. The plural is pronounced sih-KWEE-lee.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it usually refers to a lasting problem after illness or injury.
nuance.usage_note: Sequela is used mostly in medicine and in health reports. Americans almost always use the plural sequelae when discussing lasting effects of a disease, such as after COVID-19 or a stroke. In everyday talk they say 'long-term effects' or 'lasting problems'.

distinctions.note: A sequel is a book, film or story that continues an earlier work, while a sequela is a medical condition that follows an illness.
A complication is a new problem arising during treatment or illness, while a sequela is a lasting effect that comes after it.
A symptom is a current sign of illness, while a sequela is a consequence that appears later.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still has some sequelae from his stroke, like weakness in his left hand.
examples.professional: The health department report tracks the sequelae of surgery in patients over sixty-five.
examples.analytical: The philosopher treated the rise of nationalism as a sequela of the treaty rather than its cause.

nuance.analogy: A sequela is like the aftershock that follows an earthquake, a lasting result of an earlier event.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sequela, 'consequence,' from sequi, 'to follow.'
common_mistakes: Using the singular sequela when speaking of several effects; in American English the plural sequelae is more common.
Confusing sequela with sequel, which means a continuation of a story or film.

sequela.etymology: Latin *sequēla* (“aftermath, sequel; consequence, result”), from *sequor* (“to follow; to come or go after, pursue”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **sekʷ-* (“to follow”)) + *-ēla*.

senses.definition: In a manner which uses set theory.
In the sense of set theory.

core.definition: In a way that uses set theory, the branch of mathematics that studies collections of objects and their relations.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on RET, in the middle of theoretically, and the ending -ically reduces to 'ih-kuh-lee' rather than 'ee-kal-ee'. The r-colored vowel in the second syllable is a common trap for learners.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase almost only in mathematics, logic, and philosophy of mathematics papers, lectures, and proofs. In everyday speech, people say 'in theory' instead. It is often placed before an adjective, as in 'set-theoretically equivalent'.

distinctions.note: Theoretically is general and can mean in principle; set theoretically restricts the claim to the framework of set theory.
Axiomatically means derived from stated axioms; set theoretically refers specifically to the subject matter of sets.
Logically refers to valid reasoning in general, while set theoretically names the domain in which the reasoning takes place.

examples.everyday: My friend asked me to explain infinity, so I said that set theoretically, some infinite collections are bigger than others.
examples.professional: The data team models user segments set theoretically, so overlapping cohorts are counted once and not double counted.
examples.analytical: Cantor's diagonal argument shows that the real numbers cannot be listed, a result that matters set theoretically.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting a box of mixed buttons into piles by shape rather than by what they are used for.
nuance.etymology: Set comes from Old English settan; theoretically comes from Greek theoria 'contemplation' through Latin and French.
common_mistakes: Using it in everyday speech to mean 'in theory'; in conversation, say 'in theory' instead.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in THEE-ur-et-ically; the main stress is on the syllable RET.

senses.definition: Money paid as compensation to someone whose employment is ended, often in exchange of waiver.

core.definition: Money an employer pays a worker whose job ends, often in layoffs, usually in exchange for signing a release of claims.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'SEV'. The middle syllable is r-colored and weak, and the final -ance is a reduced 'uns'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business talk, but it can carry worry when it signals a layoff.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'severance pay' or 'a severance package' when a company ends a job, often through layoffs. Workers are typically asked to sign a release or waiver before receiving it. In Britain, the term is 'redundancy pay', so use 'severance pay' in the United States.

distinctions.note: Unemployment benefits come from a government program, while severance pay comes from the employer.
The final paycheck pays for hours already worked, while severance pay is extra compensation for ending the job.

examples.everyday: They offered me three months of severance pay if I agreed to sign the release.
examples.professional: Legal says the severance pay will be paid out over twelve weeks, subject to the release being signed.
examples.analytical: Severance pay can be read as compensation for lost employment, but in practice it also buys the employer a release of future claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a soft landing when a job ends, cushioning the fall.
nuance.etymology: From sever, from Latin separare, meaning to separate, plus the suffix -ance.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'severence'.
Saying 'sever pay', which is incorrect; the noun is 'severance'.

senses.definition: In a shabby manner.
Done poorly or ineptly.
senses.example: The landlord shabbily patched the roof, and water still dripped into the kitchen.

core.definition: In a worn, poor, or careless way; or in a mean, unfair way toward someone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SHAB, with a short a as in 'cat'. The second syllable is reduced to a quick 'ih', and the ending is 'lee', not 'bee-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say someone was 'treated shabbily' to mean they were treated unfairly or with contempt. For physical things, they say something was 'shabbily made' or 'shabbily furnished'. It is a mild but clear criticism, so use it carefully about people you work with.

distinctions.note: Poorly is a general word for low quality, while shabbily suggests carelessness or a worn, neglected look, and also mean treatment of people.
Unfairly describes a violation of fairness, whereas shabbily adds a sense of disrespect or contempt.

examples.everyday: The landlord treated us shabbily when we asked him to fix the heater.
examples.professional: The vendor handled our onboarding shabbily, and we lost two weeks of testing.
examples.analytical: The argument is shabbily reasoned, relying on anecdotes where it needs evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a coat with frayed cuffs: it still works as a coat, but it no longer looks or performs as well as it should.
nuance.etymology: Formed from shabby plus -ly; shabby comes from the noun shab, a word of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using shabbily for new but cheap products; 'poorly made' is more natural there.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'shab-BEE-lee'.

senses.definition: Without a clearly defined or identifiable shape.

core.definition: Having no clear, definite, or attractive shape or structure.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final -less is a light, reduced ending that sounds like 'lus', with no extra vowel after the p.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It can suggest unattractive, baggy, or unstructured, and it can sound unkind when describing a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shapeless most often for loose clothing, such as 'a shapeless sweater,' or for a vague mass or draft of work. Describing a person as shapeless is usually rude, so say 'baggy' or 'loose-fitting' if you mean clothing. In writing, 'shapeless' often means that an argument or plan lacks structure.

distinctions.note: Formless is more abstract or literary and suggests no form at all, while shapeless is common for describing clothing or a rough mass.
Baggy specifically describes loose-fitting clothing, while shapeless can describe clothing and also any vague or undefined thing.
Amorphous is formal or technical, especially in science or sociology, meaning lacking a definite or crystalline structure.

examples.everyday: I love that old sweater, but it's so shapeless I hardly ever wear it anymore.
examples.professional: The first draft of the proposal was a shapeless mess, so we spent a week organizing it into clear sections.
examples.analytical: The argument remains shapeless because the author never specifies which premises support the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like pizza dough before anyone has rolled it out: it has substance, but no form yet.
nuance.etymology: From shape plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without', from Old English -lēas.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'shay-PLESS'; the main stress is on the first syllable.
Confusing it with shapely, which is positive and means attractively shaped.

senses.definition: To make (the head, skin etc.) bald or (the hair) shorter by using a tool such as a razor or electric clippers to cut the hair close to the skin.
senses.example: Every morning he shaves his face with an electric razor before work.

senses.definition: To cut anything in this fashion.
senses.example: She shaved a thin layer off the bottom of the door so it would close.

senses.definition: To remove hair from one's face by this means.
senses.example: I had little time to shave this morning.

senses.definition: To cut finely, for example slices of meat.
senses.example: Ask the deli clerk to shave the ham paper-thin for sandwiches.

senses.definition: To skim along or near the surface of; to pass close to, or touch lightly, in passing.
senses.example: The hawk shaved the treetops as it glided across the meadow.

senses.definition: To reduce in size, weight, time taken etc. usually by a small amount.
senses.example: The team managed to shave two seconds off their lap time.

senses.definition: To injure by employing a knife.
senses.example: The drunk man tried to shave his rival with a switchblade outside the bar.

senses.definition: To buy (a note) at a discount greater than the legal rate of interest, or to deduct in discounting it more than the legal rate allows.
senses.example: The bank would shave the note at a rate higher than state law permitted.

senses.definition: An instance of shaving.
senses.example: I instructed the barber to give me a shave.

senses.definition: A thin slice; a shaving.
senses.example: Thin shaves of wood curled onto the workshop floor as he planed the board.

senses.definition: A hand tool, mainly for woodworking, consisting of a sharp blade with a handle at each end.
senses.example: He smoothed the oak board's rough edges with a wooden-handled shave before staining it.

senses.definition: A narrow miss or escape; a close shave.
senses.example: We had a close shave on the icy highway, but nobody was hurt.

senses.definition: An exorbitant discount on a note.
senses.example: The lender's shave on my promissory note was far above the legal limit.

senses.definition: A premium paid for an extension of the time of delivery or payment, or for the right to vary a stock contract in any particular.
senses.example: The broker charged a shave for extending the delivery date on the grain contract.

core.definition: To cut hair close to the skin with a razor or clippers, especially on your face, head or legs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the one syllable with a clear long "ay" and end with a voiced v. Do not add an extra vowel before the v, and keep the sound light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an everyday hygiene word with no strong emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shave with men's faces, legs, and heads, and with cutting hair short. People say "I need to shave" in the morning and "shave my legs" in ordinary talk. A barber or a hair salon offers a shave or a "straight razor shave" as a service. In a formal setting, one might say "I am clean-shaven" instead.

distinctions.note: Trim means cutting hair or beard a little shorter, while shave means removing all of it close to the skin.
Cut is a general word for cutting hair in any way, while shave specifically means close removal near the skin.

examples.everyday: I always shave before a job interview, because I want to look sharp.
examples.professional: Our team lead asked us to shave off the extra branding costs by consolidating the vendors.
examples.analytical: The Levitical rite of cleansing requires the one healed of a skin disease to shave all his hair, marking a change of status before the community.

nuance.analogy: Like smoothing a rough board with a plane until the surface is clean and even.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sceafan, to scrape or cut off.
common_mistakes: Using "shave" for cutting hair in general; Americans usually say "cut" or "trim" for hair on the head.
Confusing shave with shove, which means to push forcefully.
nuance.biblical_note: Numbers 6:5 in the RSV says that during a Nazirite vow no razor shall come upon the head, so the hair must grow. Leviticus 14:9 requires a person being cleansed from a skin disease to shave off all his hair, marking the end of his isolation. 2 Samuel 10:4-5 describes David's servants having half their beards shaved off in shame, which led to great humiliation.

shave.etymology: Middle English *shaven*, *schaven*, from Old English *sċafan* (“to shave, scrape, shred, polish”), from **skaban*, from Proto-Germanic **skabaną* (“to scrape”), from Proto-Indo-European **skabʰ-* (“to cut, split, form, carve”).

senses.definition: To alter as a side effect.
senses.example: Changing the sampling rate could side-effect the accuracy of our forecasting model.

core.definition: An unintended secondary effect of a drug, treatment, or action, often unwanted.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word on side, and put the second stress on the second syllable of effect. The first syllable of effect is unstressed and reduced to a short ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative in medical contexts, neutral in technical or engineering contexts where the unintended effect is simply noted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use side effect in conversations about medicine, such as 'Did the pills have any side effects?' In technical work, the phrase describes an unplanned change in a system. The usual American spelling is hyphenated in older texts but often written as two words now, so check the style of your document.

distinctions.note: An effect is any result; a side effect is a secondary result that was not the main goal.
A consequence can be planned or serious; a side effect is a minor or unintended extra effect.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the nausea is a common side effect, so it should go away in a few days.
examples.professional: The refactor had a side effect on the logging module, so we need to test it before the release.
examples.analytical: Every intervention in a complex system carries side effects that may be harder to anticipate than the intended outcome.

nuance.analogy: A side effect is like a ripple from a stone thrown into a pond: the stone was aimed at one spot, but the water moves everywhere.
nuance.etymology: Side from Old English side; effect from Latin effectus, from efficere (to bring about).
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally; the stress is on side and effect's second syllable.
Using side effect as a verb in standard American writing; it is a noun, though the source lists a verb sense.

conversation.text: The main side effect is that it makes you sleepy.
I had no side effects from the flu shot.
Read the label for the side effects before you take it.

senses.definition: A measure of how likely it is to draw a false conclusion in a statistical test, when the results are really just random variations.
senses.example: We set the significance level at 0.05 before collecting any data for the trial.

senses.definition: The probability, usually expressed as a percentage, of making a decision to reject the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true; the probability of making a type I error.
senses.example: With a significance level of 0.01, we reject the null hypothesis only with strong evidence.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see significance,‎ level.

core.definition: In statistics, the threshold probability, often 0.05, of wrongly rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true.

pronunciation.tip: Both words keep their stress: 'NIF' in the first, and 'LEV' in the second. Do not say 'lev-EL'; the second word is a stressed 'LEV' followed by a reduced 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term that carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'significance level' in data science, research papers, A/B testing, and statistics classes. It is usually written as the Greek letter alpha, often 0.05 or 0.01. In meetings, a data scientist might say 'We used a significance level of 0.05' to define a threshold for a result. Everyday speakers rarely use this term.

distinctions.note: The p-value is the observed probability from the data, while the significance level is the threshold chosen before the test to compare with it.
The confidence level is one minus the significance level, expressed as a percentage, so a 95 percent confidence level corresponds to a 0.05 significance level.

examples.everyday: My friend said the study was valid because it used a standard significance level.
examples.professional: We set the significance level at 0.05 before running the A/B test, so the team agreed on the threshold in advance.
examples.analytical: Choosing a significance level is a judgment about how much risk of a false positive a field is willing to accept, not a purely mathematical fact.

nuance.analogy: A significance level is like a bouncer's rule at a door: it decides in advance how much unlikely evidence is enough to let a claim in.
nuance.etymology: 'Significance' comes from Latin 'significare', to make known, and 'level' comes from Latin 'libella', a small balance.
common_mistakes: Confusing the significance level with the p-value, which is calculated from the data.
Saying 'significant level' with an adjective instead of the noun 'significance level'.

senses.definition: To model, replicate, duplicate the behavior, appearance or properties of.
senses.example: We will use a smoke machine to simulate the fog you will actually encounter.

core.definition: To imitate the behavior, appearance or conditions of something, often with a model or computer, in order to study or train.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SIM. The middle syllable is weak, like 'yuh', and the final -ate is pronounced 'ayt', not 'ut'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use. It turns negative when it means faking something, as in simulate an injury.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use simulate for models and training, such as flight simulators and stress tests. In everyday talk it can mean pretending or faking, which sounds deceptive. For casual speech, Americans often say model, copy or fake.

distinctions.note: Imitate means copy an action or style; simulate usually means reproducing the behavior of a system so it can be studied or tested.
Pretend implies deliberately deceiving or playing a role; simulate can be neutral, as in a scientific model.
Emulate means try to equal or surpass a model you admire; simulate focuses on reproducing behavior.

examples.everyday: The trainers at the gym simulate a race so you get used to the pace.
examples.professional: We need to simulate peak traffic on the staging server before the launch.
examples.analytical: Ethicists ask whether a machine that merely simulates understanding actually understands anything.

nuance.analogy: A flight simulator lets a pilot practice landings without leaving the ground.
nuance.etymology: From Latin simulare, to imitate or pretend, from similis, like.
common_mistakes: Confusing simulate with stimulate, which means to excite or encourage.
Using simulate for simple copying; in American usage it implies reproducing how a system behaves.

simulate.etymology: Latin *simulātus*, perfect passive participle of *simulō* (“make like, imitate, copy, represent, feign”) (see *-ate*), from *similis* (“like”).

senses.definition: The outer protective layer of the body of any animal, including of a human.
senses.example: He is so disgusting he makes my skin crawl.

senses.definition: The outer protective layer of the fruit of a plant.
The skin and fur of an individual animal used by humans for clothing, upholstery, etc.
senses.example: The trapper sold the beaver skins to a fur buyer in the spring.

senses.definition: A congealed layer on the surface of a liquid.
senses.example: In order to get to the rest of the paint in the can, you′ll have to remove the skin floating on top of it.

core.definition: The outer layer of the body that covers people and animals and protects them from the environment.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i, as in 'kin', and do not add a vowel between s and k or stretch the vowel into 'skeen'. The final n is a clear nasal sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to the body or to food, but in phrases like 'thick-skinned' or 'get under my skin' the meaning shifts to emotions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'skin' for the body's outer covering and 'peel' for the outer layer of most fruits and vegetables, though 'skin' is used for chicken, fish and potatoes. 'Get under my skin' means to annoy someone, and 'thick-skinned' means not easily hurt by criticism. In a doctor's office, 'skin' is a neutral everyday word, while 'dermatology' is the medical field.

distinctions.note: Complexion refers to the color and texture of the face; skin is the whole body covering.
Hide is the thick skin of a large animal, used to make leather; skin is the everyday word for a person's or animal's outer covering.
Peel is the outer layer of fruit or vegetables that you remove; skin is used for the covering of chicken or fish.

examples.everyday: My skin gets really dry in the winter, so I put lotion on every morning.
examples.professional: Customers with sensitive skin should avoid this product, so the label needs a clear warning.
examples.analytical: Philosophers who study perception often treat the skin as the boundary between the self and the world, which makes touch central to theories of embodiment.

nuance.analogy: Skin is like a waterproof jacket that is also alive: it keeps the inside in and the outside out, and it repairs itself.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse skinn, meaning animal hide or skin.
common_mistakes: Using skin for fruit and vegetables, where Americans usually say peel
Adding an extra vowel, as in 'skin-ih', when pronouncing the word
Confusing skin with skim, which is pronounced similarly but has a different meaning

skin.etymology: From Middle English *skyn*, *skinn*, from Old English *scinn*, from Old Norse *skinn* (“animal hide”), from Proto-Germanic **skinþą*, from Proto-Indo-European **sken-* (“to split off”), nasal variant of **skeh₁i-d-* (“to cut”).

senses.definition: An imaginary place inhabited by those who are asleep; the state of slumber.

core.definition: An imaginary place of sleep and dreams; a playful way to describe the state of being asleep.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SLUM and the second part, 'land,' has a lighter secondary stress. The 'er' is r-colored, so pronounce it as a single syllable with no separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive and whimsical. It suggests peaceful sleep and a fairy-tale quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'slumberland' mostly in children's stories, bedtime talk, or playful expressions, such as 'Time to go to Slumberland.' It is best known from the comic strip 'Little Nemo in Slumberland.' Adults usually say 'dreamland' or 'the land of nod' in everyday speech, and 'slumberland' sounds whimsical or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Dreamland' is the more common phrase for the world of dreams; 'slumberland' emphasizes deep, peaceful sleep and sounds more playful.
'The land of nod' is an informal, common idiom for falling asleep; 'slumberland' is more whimsical and less common.

examples.everyday: Okay, kids, it's time to head off to Slumberland, so brush your teeth and hop in bed.
examples.professional: The offsite is over, so let's wrap up and not turn the call into a trip to Slumberland.
examples.analytical: The term 'slumberland' personifies sleep as a place, which reveals how the imagination turns rest into a kind of journey.

nuance.analogy: Slumberland is like a bedtime map: a place you travel to each night and then return from by morning.
nuance.etymology: From slumber plus land; a whimsical compound popularized by Winsor McCay's comic strip 'Little Nemo in Slumberland' (1905).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'slumber party,' which is a social event where people sleep over.
Using it as a serious term for sleep disorders, when it's a playful or literary phrase.

senses.definition: In which smoking is not allowed.
senses.example: This entire restaurant is smoke-free.

core.definition: Describing a place or building where smoking is not allowed, such as a restaurant, office or apartment.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on FREE, the second word, and SMOKE has a lighter stress. Make the r in free clear, and keep the long ee sound in the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is usually used to promote healthy air and comfort for nonsmokers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smoke-free on signs, rental listings, restaurant menus and building policies, and it is the normal way to describe a place where smoking is banned. People say a restaurant is smoke-free or that they want a smoke-free apartment. Nonsmoking is also common, especially for seats or sections, but smoke-free describes the whole place.

distinctions.note: Nonsmoking often refers to a section or seat for people who do not smoke, while smoke-free describes a whole place where smoking is banned.
Tobacco-free is broader and can include vaping or chewing tobacco, while smoke-free usually refers only to burning tobacco.

examples.everyday: We're looking for a smoke-free apartment, so please tell me if the building allows smoking.
examples.professional: The company adopted a smoke-free policy for all campuses last year, which applies to employees and visitors.
examples.analytical: A smoke-free ordinance changes behavior less by punishment than by redefining the shared air as a public good.

nuance.analogy: A smoke-free place is like a room with a clear window: the air is open and no one is blocked from breathing it comfortably.
common_mistakes: Saying smoke-free with the stress on SMOKE, which sounds unnatural to Americans.
Confusing smoke-free with nonsmoking when describing a whole building, where smoke-free is more precise.
